Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 31, verse 1:

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

We have already explained at length the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of the surahs, and we mentioned everything that a human being could say about them. After all of that, we say: God knows best what He intends by them, for however much knowledge we are given, we will never reach the ultimate meaning of these letters, and there will remain meanings in them that we are unable to attain.

If you say: what is the benefit of these disjointed letters if their meaning is not known? We reply: we are debating with you by means of reason and logic. The Qur'an was revealed in the Arabic style, and it challenged the Arabs, who were the people of eloquence, rhetoric, and clear expression, the masters of beautiful speech and superb delivery. It was revealed among the Quraysh, whose language combined all the dialects of the Arab tribes, and from them came the mighty chieftains who denied Muhammad and rejected his call. Have we ever heard any of them say, for example: what is the meaning of (Alif Lam Mim) or (Ha Mim)?

By God, if there had been any flaw in them, they would not have left it alone. Therefore, this is evidence that they understood these letters and knew that they have a meaning. At the very least, we may say that they are among the particles of alerting (huruf al-tanbih) that the Arabs used in their speech, like (ala) in the words of the poet:(1)

Ala, awake with your cup and bring us morning wine, and do not withhold the wine of al-Andarin.(2)

So "ala" is a particle of alerting. The importance of alerting at the beginning of speech lies in the fact that the speaker holds the reins of his argument, arranges it and prepares it, and manages his points in mental order within his mind, but the listener may be heedless and be surprised by the speech without preparation, so something escapes him. Thus the particles of alerting come to take him out of his heedlessness and attract his attention, so that nothing of your speech escapes him. Therefore, the least that can be said about these letters is that they serve to alert, in the manner of the Arabs in their speech.

We have already shown that the Qur'an is entirely built on continuity (al-wasl) in its verses and surahs, indeed at its end and its beginning. We say: (from the jinn and mankind) (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful) (Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds), and likewise in the verses and surahs. It is as if God, exalted is He, wants you not to separate a verse of the Qur'an from the one that follows it. Therefore they say of the reciter of the Qur'an: he is the "halting traveler" (al-hal al-murtahil): he is in one verse or surah, and moves on to the one that follows it.

So continuity is a general characteristic of the entire Qur'an, with no exception except the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs, which are based on separation. So we do not say here "alif lam mim" in continuous form, but we say "alif, lam, mim." Why have these letters differed from the general characteristic of the whole Qur'an?

They said: to show you that alif, or lam, or mim, each has its own independent meaning, and they are not mere letters like the other letters of the Qur'an. Therefore they departed from the Qur'anic pattern of continuity, because each has an independent meaning that it conveys.

This is explained by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites a letter of the Book of God, he has for it a good deed, and a good deed is multiplied tenfold. I do not say that alif lam mim is one letter, but alif is a letter, lam is a letter, and mim is a letter."(3)

1 He is: Amr ibn Kulthum ibn Malik ibn Attab, Abu al-Aswad, a pre-Islamic poet, born in the north of the Arabian Peninsula in the lands of Rabi'a, who travelled there, in al-Sham, Iraq and Najd. He was among the bold and fearless warriors. His most famous poetry is his mu'allaqa, in which this verse appears. He died around 40 BH. [al-A'lam by al-Zirikli 5/84].
2 Al-sahn: a large drinking bowl; al-Andarun: villages in al-Sham. The meaning of the verse: "Ala, awake from your sleep, O cupbearer, and fill the morning-drink in your great bowl, and do not hoard the wine of these villages." [Sharh al-Mu'allaqat al-sab' by al-Zawzani, p. 165].
3 Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2910) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and he said: this is a hasan sahih gharib hadith from this route.

Then Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ (2).

*Tilka* (تلك) is a demonstrative pronoun for the feminine, as *dhalika* (ذلك) is for the masculine. It consists of the *ta'* (ت) for pointing, and the *lam* (ل) for distance, whether distance in place or in rank and standing. Then the *kaf* (ك) marks the addressee, and it varies according to the addressee: masculine or feminine, singular, dual or plural.

So you say, addressing a single masculine person: *tilka*. For a single feminine person: *tilki*. For the dual: *tilkuma*... and so on. From this is the saying of the wife of the Governor concerning Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ (32) [Yusuf]. Here *dha* (ذا) is the demonstrative referring to Joseph, the *lam* marks distance, and *kunna* (كنّ) is the pronoun addressing a feminine plural.

And He says, addressing Moses: ﴿Those two are two proofs from your Lord﴾ (32) [al-Qasas], meaning the hand and the staff. *Dhanani* (فذانِ) is the demonstrative for the dual, and the *kaf* is the address.

The demonstrative here, ﴿These are the verses...﴾ (2) [Luqman], refers to a feminine noun, namely *al-ayat* (the verses). The addressee is our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his community follows him. The Noble Qur'an sometimes refers to the verses and sometimes refers to the Book itself, so it says "the Book," or "the Criterion" (al-Furqan), or "the Qur'an," and each of these has its own meaning.

"The Book" indicates that it is written and contained in lines. "The Qur'an" indicates that it is recited and contained in hearts. As for "the Criterion" (al-Furqan), this is the task it performs: to distinguish between truth and falsehood.

Here He says: ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ (2) [Luqman], so He describes it with wisdom. But at the beginning of al-Baqarah He says: ﴿That is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance...﴾ (2) [al-Baqarah]. There it is not described with wisdom, rather it is denied that there is any doubt in it, that is, any uncertainty.

The phrase ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ (2) [al-Baqarah] confirms for us the truthfulness of the Messenger in conveying from Allah, and the truthfulness of the angel who carried it from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to the Messenger of Allah. Allah has praised him by saying: ﴿Possessor of power, with esteem in the presence of the Lord of the Throne﴾ (20) [al-Takwir].

And concerning our master, the Messenger of Allah, regarding the conveying of the Qur'an, He says: ﴿And if he had made up about Us some sayings (44), We would have seized him by the right hand (45), then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾ (46) [al-Haqqah].

Therefore: the Qur'an, as it was revealed from Allah, not a single letter of it has been changed, and it will remain so, preserved by Allah's preservation of it until the Hour arrives. We will continue to recite ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ (2) [al-Baqarah].

Those after us will recite it until the Hour arrives. Allah, glorified is He, has decreed that there is no doubt in this Qur'an from the time it was revealed until the Hour arrives. So if we have doubts about anything in the Book of our Lord, then we must recite ﴿That is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ (2) [al-Baqarah].

This is a matter Allah has decreed, and it extends and remains as long as the world remains, as we have already said in His saying: ﴿We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves...﴾ (53) [Fussilat]. The verse encompasses the whole future: the future of those who lived at the time the Qur'an was revealed, the future of those who come after them until the Hour arrives, and indeed the future of those upon whom the Hour will arise.

Allah did not send down the Qur'an to exhaust all its secrets and all its miracles in one century, nor in one nation, and then face the other centuries and nations without giving. Allah wants the Qur'an to remain new, so that every nation and every age may take from it, and stand upon its secrets, its miracles, and its signs in the universe.

The meaning of ﴿the Wise Book﴾ (2) [Luqman]: the Book is not described as wise; rather, wisdom is an attribute of one who knows. So the meaning is: the Wise Book, that is, the one described with wisdom; or the wise one who speaks it; or the wise one who sent it down. The meaning of *hakim* (حكيم, wise) is one who places a thing in its proper place, and none places a thing in its proper place except Allah, because He is the one who knows the true rightness of a thing in its place.

As for us, we are guided to the place of a thing, but then its error in its place becomes clear to us, and we are compelled to change it or adjust it, like many inventions that we thought would serve humanity, and then we saw their harms, and were burned by their fire afterwards.

So each verse mentions an aspect of the perfection of the Qur'an and a direction of its greatness. Therefore these are different snapshots of one thing that has many qualities of perfection. Likewise you find the multiplicity of perfections in the verse after it: ﴿a guidance and a mercy for the good-doers﴾ (3).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 31, verse 3:

Here He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Guidance and mercy for the doers of good (31:3)﴾. But at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah He says: ﴿Guidance for the God-conscious (2:2)﴾. There is a difference between the two meanings. Taqwa (God-consciousness) necessitates faith (iman), and what faith requires is obligation (al-iftirad), meaning that you perform what Allah has made obligatory upon you.

As for what ihsan (excellence, doing good) requires, it is above that. Ihsan in performance means that you excel in its quantity and that you excel in its quality. You excel in its quality by accompanying the deed with sincerity (ikhlas) toward the One for whom the deed is done, who is Allah, glory be to Him. You excel in its quantity by loving the obligation so much that you perform more than what has been prescribed for you. Instead of praying two rak'ahs, you pray three or four. This is excellence in quantity.

Taqwa is among the wonders of Qur'anic interpretation (ta'wil), as we have said before. The Qur'an says ﴿Fear Allah (ittaqu Allah)﴾ and it says ﴿Guard yourselves against the Fire (ittaqu al-nar)﴾, and the meaning upon careful examination is one, because "ittaqi al-nar" means: place between yourself and it a shield and a barrier that protects you from it. Likewise "ittaqi Allah" does not mean that you place a barrier between yourself and your Lord, because the believer is always in the company of Allah.

Rather, place between yourself and the attributes of majesty (sifat al-jalal) and their objects from Allah a shield. Guard yourself against the attributes of the Avenger, the Compeller, the Subduer... etc., because you are not able to bear these attributes. There is no doubt that the Fire is one of the soldiers of Allah and one of the objects of the attributes of majesty. Thus the meaning is one.

Some take the apparent sense and say: how do we guard ourselves against Allah, when taqwa means keeping away something harmful from you? We say: yes, you keep away from yourself disbelief, and this is the very essence of taqwa. The God-conscious are those who love to guard themselves toward Allah by not being disbelievers in Him. As long as a person has guarded himself against disbelief, he is a doer of good and a believer. The Qur'an sometimes mentions the necessary consequence and sometimes the thing necessitating it, so that each conveys a new meaning.

Therefore, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about ihsan in the hadith of Jibril, he said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, [know that] He sees you" (1).

When we compare the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah with this verse ﴿Guidance and mercy for the doers of good (31:3)﴾, we see that the Qur'an does not rest on repetition.

Rather, these are miraculous glimpses, each of which conveys a meaning. Although a superficial glance may suppose it is repetition, in reality it is new bounty if you reflect upon it.

Here the Book is described as wise (hakim), and as guidance and mercy. Guidance (huda) is pointing to good by the shortest path. The Qur'an was sent to guide a people who had gone astray. When it guided them to the right course and showed them the light, He wished to preserve this guidance for them and that they not turn away from it, so He said ﴿and mercy (wa rahmah)﴾. That is: among Allah's mercy toward them is that they not return to error again.

As in His saying: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers (17:82)﴾. The meaning: healing for one who was ill, and mercy so that he never falls ill again afterward.

(1) A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). It was narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (50) and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (8), from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab, and it is the lengthy hadith of Jibril, who appeared in the form of a man "of exceedingly white clothing and exceedingly black hair, on whom no trace of travel was seen, and none of us knew him," and he asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about Islam, iman, and ihsan..

Then Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿Those who establish prayer and give zakat, and they, of the Hereafter, are certain.﴾

This verse came as a description of the muhsinun (the doers of good). Is this all their qualities, that they establish prayer, give zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter? They say: No, but these qualities are the fundamental pillars, and Allah, the Exalted, wants from His creation equality in servitude ('ubudiyyah), and this equality is not achieved except when all are equal.

In prayer in particular this equality is manifested, and in it appears the might of lordship and the humility of servitude, and in it is the utmost submission to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Then it is repeated five times in the day and night.

As for the other obligations, they do not take this form. Zakat, for example, is due once a year: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-An'am: 141], and it is obligatory only upon the one who is able, and not on others. Likewise fasting and hajj. So it is as if prayer is the pillar of all acts of worship, and because of its nobility and station Allah made it binding upon the servant and never let it fall from him in any circumstance. Therefore the prayer of the sick, the traveller, and the one in fear was legislated, etc.

In prayer there is a flattening out of servitude among all creatures, for we take off our ranks when we take off our shoes at the door of the mosque. In one row stand the leader and the led, the elder and the young, the high and the low—meaning the one who is lowly in the eyes of people, and perhaps he is not lowly in the sight of his Lord. All here are equal. Then when we see the great, the leaders and the lords standing with us in the rows, submissive to Allah and humbled, the distinctions between us vanish, and pride is crushed in their souls, so that no one exalts himself over anyone in the society of the Muslims.

And because of the station and importance of prayer, we have seen how it is the only obligation which Allah imposed upon us directly. As for the rest of the duties, they were imposed through revelation. We had previously given an example of this with the head of a workplace when an important matter comes to him: he does not order it by letter or by telephone, but summons the competent employee to his office and conveys the order to him directly.

Likewise, the Messenger of Allah was summoned by his Lord to the heavens, and he took a share of nearness to Allah, the Exalted. Allah, glorified is He, knows the Messenger's love for his community and his eagerness for them, and that they too should attain this nearness to His presence. So his Lord answered him, and made prayer a presence of the servant in His presence, and a nearness like the nearness of the Messenger of Allah during the Mi'raj journey.

Therefore his Lord addressed him saying: ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied.﴾ [al-Duha: 5]

So our master, the Messenger of Allah, said: "Then, I will not be satisfied while one of my community is in the Fire."(1)

Just as prayer produces a flattening out of servitude, zakat produces in society an economic flattening, so that all live—rich and poor—a dignified and comfortable life. No one is satiated to the point of excess while another dies of hunger. And what of a society in which the great does not exalt himself over the small, and the rich does not withhold from the poor? Thus in prayer and zakat there is what guarantees the happiness of the whole society.

Allah imposed zakat for the poor, because when Allah summons His servant to His existence, He must guarantee for him the necessities of life. And why not? When you invite someone to your home, you must honour him and at least prepare for him the necessities of what he requires, beyond honour and hospitality and the luxury of food and drink, etc.

So Allah, glorified is He, summoned His servants into existence, believers and disbelievers alike, and it is incumbent upon Him to provide them with sustenance, indeed all the necessities of their lives. Likewise He guarantees the sustenance of the one who is incapable and unable. Therefore He imposed zakat as a known right for the beggar and the deprived. So zakat is a connection (sila), and prayer is the first of them.

There is a story about this matter in Arabic literature. It is related that Ibn al-Mudabbir, whose kunya was Abu al-Hasan, was approached by poets seeking to obtain his gifts. They would say: "Verily al-laha opens mouths (al-laha taftah al-laha)"(2), meaning: gifts open the mouths with praise and commendation.

But when a poet praised him with a poem that did not please him, Ibn al-Mudabbir would order his men to take him to the mosque and not leave him until he had prayed a hundred rak'ahs to Allah. Thus the poets feared him and avoided going to him, except Abu 'Abd Allah al-Husayn ibn 'Abd al-Salam al-Bushra, who went to him and said: "I have a poem which I would love to recite to you." He said: "Do you know the condition?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Say what you have." So he said:

We desired in Abu al-Hasan praise, as rulers are sought with praise for their bounties.

That is, poets go to them to obtain their goodness.

So we said: "Honour of the two weights in full, and from whose palms the Tigris and the Euphrates [flow]."

And they said: "He accepts praise, but his gifts are upon them—prayer."

So I said to them: "What does my prayer avail my dependants? The matter is only zakat."

Then he orders for me the breaking of its sad (ṣ), so the ṣalawāt become for me the ṣalāh.

When one of them became bold toward him and asked: "Why do you punish with a hundred rak'ahs the one whose poetry does not please you?" He said: "Because he is either a wrongdoer or a doer of good. If he is a wrongdoer, then it is an expiation for his evil in his poetry; and if he is a doer of good, then it is an expiation for his lying about me."

Then He, glorified is He, says in describing them: ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, they are certain﴾ [Luqman: 4], because belief in the Last Day requires that we act according to the method of Allah in "do such and such" and "do not do such and such," while we are certain that we shall not escape from Allah nor flee from His punishment in the Hereafter, and that we shall be held accountable for our deeds. We were not created in vain, nor will we be left neglected, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115].

We notice here in the style the repetition of the pronoun of the third person (hum), as He said: ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, they are certain﴾ [Luqman: 4], and this indicates that belief in the Hereafter is an affirmed matter with no doubt about it. Although people believe in this day, and believe that they will be held accountable, and that Allah did not impose upon them in vain, yet the Exalted emphasises the matter of the Hereafter, because it is a remote matter in the eyes of people, and they may be heedless of it due to its distance from them. Why not, when they are heedless even of death, which they see before them every day? But it is the habit of man to consider it remote as regards himself.

Therefore al-Hasan al-Basri(3) said: "I have never seen a certainty more like doubt than people's certainty about death."

As for the disbelievers, they deny this day and do not believe in it; therefore Allah emphasised it.

When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked Hudhayfah(4), may Allah be pleased with him: "How have you woken up, O Hudhayfah?" He said: "I have woken up a true believer." He said: "Every truth has a reality; what is the reality of your faith?" He said: "My soul has turned away from this world, so its gold and its clay are equal to me, and it is as if I were looking at the people of Paradise in Paradise enjoying bliss, and at the people of the Fire in the Fire being tormented." The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "You have known; then hold fast."

His saying ﴿they are certain﴾ [Luqman: 4] is from yaqin (certainty), which is firm faith that does not waver, and into which no doubt enters so that it rises to the intellect to be debated afresh. We have previously said that knowledge progresses through three stages: 'ilm al-yaqin (knowledge of certainty), 'ayn al-yaqin (eye of certainty), and haqq al-yaqin (truth of certainty).

'Ilm al-yaqin is when one whom you trust tells you about it; when you see what he told you, it is 'ayn al-yaqin; and when you experience it yourself, it is haqq al-yaqin.

We gave an example of this: if I tell you that the Sacred House is in Makkah and describe it so-and-so, and that expansions have been made to it such-and-such, then this information for you is 'ilm al-yaqin. When you see the Haram, it is 'ayn al-yaqin. When Allah facilitates for you the Hajj or 'Umrah and you experience it yourself, it is haqq al-yaqin.

The Exalted, glorified is He, addressed these levels in two surahs: ﴿Competition in increase diverts you, until you visit the graves. No! You are going to know. Then no! You are going to know. No! If you knew with the knowledge of certainty, you would surely see the Hellfire. Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty. Then you will surely be asked that Day about pleasure﴾ [al-Takathur: 1–8].

That is when they pass over the Sirat and see the Fire with their own eyes.

As for haqq al-yaqin regarding the Fire, it came in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if he was among those brought near, then rest and provision and a Garden of pleasure. And if he was among the companions of the right, then peace be upon you from the companions of the right. But if he was among the deniers, the astray, then a welcome of boiling water and burning in Hellfire. Indeed, this is the truth of certainty. So exalt the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88–96].

But is the Qur'an revealed only as guidance for the God-fearing and for the doers of good? We have said: guidance comes in two senses: guidance of indication and direction, and guidance of enabling and assistance. If it is guidance of indication, then Allah indicated to both believer and disbeliever, by His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

So the Exalted gave guidance to all because they are His servants. Some accepted the indication and were convinced by it and believed, and some rejected it and disbelieved. As for the one who accepted Allah's indication and believed in Him, Allah increases him in another guidance, which is help in faith: He makes it beloved to him until he loves it, then He helps him to it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And those who are guided—He increases them in guidance and gives them their righteousness﴾ [Muhammad: 17].

(1) Al-Khatib narrated in *Talkhis al-Mutashabih* from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Muhammad will not be satisfied while one of his community is in the Fire." And al-Bayhaqi narrated in *Shu'ab al-Iman* from Ibn 'Abbas also that he said: "His satisfaction is that his entire community enter Paradise."

(2) *Al-laha*: the best and most abundant of gifts. It is said: "He is indeed generous with al-laha" when he is a munificent man who gives much. *Al-lahah*: a red fleshy part in the palate at the far end of the roof of the mouth. [Lisan al-'Arab, root l-h-w].

(3) He is al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan Abu Sa'id al-Basri. He grew up in Madinah, memorised the Book during the caliphate of 'Uthman, and heard him preach several times. He was a lofty scholar, trustworthy, a proof, a model, devout and ascetic, abundant in knowledge, eloquent, and handsome. He died in the year 110 AH at the age of eighty-eight. [Tadhkirat al-Huffaz by al-Dhahabi 1/71].

(4) What was reported concerns al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari. Al-Haythami cited it in *Majma' al-Zawa'id* (1/57), attributing it to al-Tabarani in *al-Mu'jam al-Kabir* (3/302), and said: "In it is Ibn Lahi'ah." He also cited it from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, met a man called Harithah in one of the lanes of Madinah and said: "How have you woken up, O Harithah?" — the hadith — and attributed it to al-Bazzar, in which is Yusuf ibn 'Atiyyah, whose narration is not used as proof.

(5) *Al-madr*: pieces of dried clay; it is the clay that holds together. [Lisan al-'Arab, root m-d-r].

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾

The Truth, glorified is He, described His Qur'an as guidance. Here, however, He says: ﴿Those are upon guidance﴾ [Luqman]. The One speaking is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so we must reflect on the meaning. Our Lord, Mighty and Majestic, wants to tell us: yes, the Qur'an is guidance. But beware of thinking that when you follow this guidance you benefit it with anything. Rather, the one who benefits from guidance is you. When you are upon guidance, it points you out and carries you towards good. Guidance is like a mount that brings you to goodness and righteousness. You are the one who rises through guidance if you accept it, even though it is the One who is exalted above it in legislation.

Then, guidance from whom? ﴿A guidance from their Lord﴾ [Luqman], from One who is not corrected. If He guides you, He guides you with truth. Suppose that human beings have arrived at something containing good; yet after a period they themselves oppose this path, discover for it harms and defects, correct it, and perhaps turn away from it to something else. And how many human laws have been cancelled or amended?

So then: true guidance and true direction belong only to Allah, and the law by which we ought to be governed and in which we can be at peace belongs only to Allah. Why? Because human beings may benefit from their own laws, desires may control them, or they may incline toward one person at the expense of another. As for the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, He alone is the One who benefits from nothing of what He has legislated for His servants, and He shows favouritism to no one at the expense of another. All the servants are His servants, and they are equal before Him.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, reassures us about His legislation and His justice, saying: ﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾ [al-Jinn]. That is: be at ease, for your Lord has no consort who could influence Him, nor a son who would wrong people by favouring him. You are all equal before Him.

Then there is a difference between guidance from Allah and guidance from the Lord (rabb). The Lord is the One who raised you. He is the One who brought you into existence from nothingness, sustained you from nothingness, gave you before you knew to ask, and left you to dwell in His dominion and enjoy His blessings.

Therefore your Lord teaches you: beware of asking Me for tomorrow's provision, for I provided for you before you knew how to ask. Then I did not require of you tomorrow's worship. So let the servant be courteous with his Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

Thus we see that lordship (rububiyyah) is a bestowal, while divinity (uluhiyyah) is an obligation.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, informs us of another matter about them: ﴿and those are the successful﴾ [Luqman]. Success (falah) is the result of the guidance which they followed and adhered to, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Mu'minun].

Falah originally derives from the cultivation of the land by ploughing, sowing, irrigating, and so on. The Qur'anic style borrowed it for righteous action, and the point of resemblance between the two matters is clear: the farmer casts the seed, and his Lord multiplies it for him seven hundred times. Likewise, righteous action is multiplied for its doer, for the good deed with Allah is ten times its like up to seven hundred fold: ﴿and Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah].

And read in the Book of Allah this parable: ﴿The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven spikes; in each spike is a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing and Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah].

And reflect on the argument here: if the earth, which is created by Allah, gives all this bounty, how then can the giving of the One who created it be? Therefore, without doubt, they are successful, that is, they win the good fruit which exceeds the effort they exerted, just as the farmer ploughs the land and it gives him many times what he placed in it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 31, verse 6:

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And among the people is one who buys idle talk to mislead [others] from the way of Allah without knowledge and takes it in ridicule. For those there will be a humiliating punishment.﴾

After Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the Book and its verses, and that in it there is guidance and mercy for whoever follows it and success for whoever walks in its guidance, He shows us that there is another kind of people who profit from misguidance and benefit from it; otherwise its market would not thrive, nor would it have spread among people in various forms and colours.

Therefore we see that misguidance has a particular group whose interest is that it continue and spread, so that their gains remain, their lordship over creation remains, their enslavement of people remains, and the draining of their goods continues.

And it is natural that when a law arises that restores the balance of righteousness to society, only these people stand against it: they fight it, fight its people, accuse them, and cast doubt upon their intentions. Indeed, they confront them with mockery and ridicule at one time and with aggression at another.

Perhaps they cut off the means of livelihood from them, just as they isolated the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the valley of Abu Talib, and they compel the people of truth to emigrate and to leave their wealth and families, once to Abyssinia and once again to Madinah. Why? Because their life rests on this misguidance, so they must preserve it.

Allah, glorified is He, shows us that those who fight the truth and stand in the way of the call to faith know full well that if they let people hear the method of Allah and the caller to goodness, people would inevitably incline towards it. Therefore they place a barrier between people's ears and the discourse of truth. They are the ones who said to the people: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it...﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

This is only because they are certain of the language of the Qur'an, the beauty of its style, and its winning of hearts through its sweet eloquence. If an Arab ear heard it, it would inevitably be affected by it, recognise the aspects of its inimitability, and end up in faith.

So if anyone among them escapes and turns to listening to the truth, they bring against him other distractions and sounds that divert him from truth to falsehood.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And among the people (6)﴾ [Luqman]: the "min" here is for partition, meaning: the people who profit from misguidance, those who are distressed that people should all follow one discourse, one aim and one guidance, because this unity would put an end to their distinction, their tyranny and their oppression on earth. Therefore they exert their utmost effort in misguidance: ﴿And among the people is one who buys idle talk to mislead [others] from the way of Allah...﴾ [Luqman: 6].

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿yashtari (buys)﴾ [Luqman: 6] derives from purchase (shira'), which is opposed to sale (bay'). Purchase is that you pay a price and take in return a priced item. This is after money has been found; but before money existed, people dealt by barter, exchanging goods for goods, and in this case every item sold is also bought, and each of the two is both seller and buyer.

Among this is the saying of the Exalted in the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few dirhams, and they were of those who had no interest in him﴾ [Yusuf: 20].

The meaning: "sharuhu" means they sold him.

Also among this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207].

That is: he sells it. So the verb (shara) comes with the meaning of selling and with the meaning of buying.

When the verb comes in the form (ishtara), it denotes purchase for which a price is paid. Among this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbly submitting to Allah, not exchanging the signs of Allah for a small price...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 199].

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for that they will have Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111].

Usually the letter "ba'" (bi) is attached to the thing given up: you say, "I bought such-and-such for such-and-such."

When we reflect on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who buys idle talk﴾ [Luqman: 6], we find that this is a process requiring seeking the thing bought, then a price to be paid for it; and would that the purchase were of something beneficial, but it is ﴿idle talk﴾ [Luqman: 6], and this is a base commodity.

So: those who want to bar [people] from the way of Allah have borne the hardship of seeking and the burden of the price, and then they are described as losers because they were content with a base commodity. More striking still, and more bitter, is that they place this in exchange for the truth that came to them from Allah through His Messenger, without toil, without hardship and without price; it came to them as a bounty and generosity from Allah: ﴿Say, I do not ask you for it any reward except affection among relatives﴾ [al-Shura: 23].

So what folly is this for which they are described!

As for the word "lahw" (idle talk/diversion): the Qur'an mentions lahw and la'b (play) in several verses. It placed la'b before lahw in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And the worldly life is but play and diversion, and the home of the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah. Then will you not reason?﴾ [al-An'am: 32].

And in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Know that the worldly life is but play and diversion﴾ [al-Hadid: 20].

And it placed lahw before la'b in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And this worldly life is but diversion and play﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64].

So the verses placed la'b first in two places, because la'b is making a movement that is not intended for any benefit, as children play; that is, a movement with no aim, and we say of it "la'b 'iyal" (children's play). It is called la'b because the child plays before being charged with anything, so he is not distracted by play from other duties.

But when he moves to the stage of responsibility, play occupies him from something demanded of him, and in this case it is called lahw. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it and leave you standing﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11].

So: lahw is that thing in which there is no benefit, and which distracts you from what is required of you.

Thus the verse of Surat al-'Ankabut, which placed lahw before la'b, means that matters of occupation with other than religion have reached a level, and that corruption has spread and become rife, and that being busy with what is not required prevails over what is required. This is a stronger meaning than placing la'b first, because la'b has not distracted him from anything.

But what is the diversion they bought in order to divert people from the truth and from the call of Islam? When they heard the Qur'an, they heard in it stories about 'Ad and Thamud, and about Madyan and Pharaoh, etc., so they wanted to occupy people with stories like these.

One of them, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, went to Persia and came to them from there with entertaining stories about Rustam, the Chosroes and the kings of Himyar. He bought them and brought them back, and he set up for himself a gathering in which people would assemble to hear him recount them, diverting them by listening from hearing the discourse of truth concerning the Messenger of Allah.

Another says: rather, one of them brought a singing girl who sang to them lewd, coquettish songs.

As for the meaning of ﴿lahw al-hadith﴾ [Luqman: 6], the scholars said: it is everything that diverts from what is required by Allah; and even if a thing is not in itself outside what Allah requires, it is lahw if it distracts from what Allah requires. Accordingly, work that diverts its doer, such as a craft, agriculture, etc., counts as lahw if it preoccupies him, for example, from prayer or from performing a duty to Allah, the Exalted.

Among conduct, there is what counts as lahw even if it does not distract you from anything, such as singing. The scholars have much to say on it, especially after it became accompanied by music, musical instruments, lewd and licentious movements. Our jurists of old had their opinion on this subject, but the modern scholars who wish to permit this matter take one angle from the words of the ancients and apply it to other than their words.

Indeed, our scholars permitted enjoyment of singing at weddings and at festivals, relying on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who saw two girls singing in the house of the Messenger of Allah and rebuked them, and said: "The flute of Satan in the house of the Messenger of Allah?" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Leave them, for it is a day of festivity."

Likewise they permitted the anashid (chants) recited to inflame the enthusiasm of soldiers in war, or those which workers chant to cheer themselves and be occupied by them from the hardships of work, or the mother who lulls her child to sleep.

Among this is the hida' (driving song) of camels to make them quicken their pace, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Anjasha: "Gently with the glass [vessels]," likening women in their delicacy and tenderness to glass. When camels hasten with them, the litters sway with them, and this is hard on the women.

So: there is no objection to every text that has a noble purpose. But if it stirs the instincts, it is forbidden, and the discussion here is of the text alone, because the Creator, glorified is He, knows the nature of human instincts; therefore we call it an instinct (gharizah), because it has activity and interaction in the soul without any external influences, and it has an energy that must move; if you stir it, it is roused and tends towards what is not praised in its outcome.

We have previously clarified that the levels of feeling are three: it is perceived by the senses, then an emotion (wijdan) forms in the soul as a result of perception, then the impulse and the action that translates this emotion.

And from Allah's mercy towards us is that the Shari'ah does not intervene in this matter except at the stage of impulse, so it says to you: "Stop, do not stretch your hand to what is not yours." We illustrated this matter with the rose that you see in the garden: it pleases you in appearance and its fragrance attracts you, so you love it, and this is yours; but if you stretch out your hand to pluck it, the Lawgiver says to you: "Stop, it is not your right."

So the wise Lawgiver does not intervene at the stage of perception, nor in emotions, except in one matter that cannot be separated between perception, emotion and impulse, because they are all one thing: it is the act of a man looking at a woman who is not lawful to him. Why this matter in particular?

They said: because it does not stop at the limit of admiration for the sight; rather, this admiration bequeaths in you a particular agitation in the soul, and a particular formation that does not calm except by your giving in to impulse. So out of mercy for you, O my servant, I will intervene in this very matter from its beginning, and prevent you from mere perception, for if you perceive you will feel, and if you feel you will be drawn to what you feel, and you will sin against people's honour, or suppress it in yourself and harm it. And your Lord wants to clear you of sin and of harm to the self; so the safest course for you is to lower your gaze.

So: do not say "singing" but say the text itself: if it urges a virtue, it is lawful; if it stirs the instincts, it is forbidden and void, like one who makes love-verses about a woman and mentions her charms; this is forbidden even without singing, and if you add to it music, melodies, coquetry and effeminacy, its prohibition increases and its sin is multiplied.

As for what we see now and hear of what they call singing, and what accompanies it of movements, dances, licentiousness and loud music, there is no doubt of its prohibition.

Everything that takes a person out of his dignity and gravity, and everything that wounds refined feelings, is forbidden. Then, singing is sound; if it departs from sound into another provocative performance, in which hands, feet, eyes and waist are used, etc., then all of this is void and forbidden.

A believer who controls his own self should not say, "They impose this on us." The believer has insight by which he is guided and distinguishes the lean from the fat, and truth from falsehood. So be a judge yourself over what you see and hear; indeed, over what your family and children see and hear. The control is in your hand: if you wish, you listen, and if you wish, you switch off the device; you have no excuse, for no one can force you to listen to or watch what you dislike.

In Ramadan, for example, which is a month of worship, we fast its days and stand in prayer through its nights, and we should honour it and maintain in it gravity and spirituality; yet they come out at us with all kinds of diversion that contradicts fasting. If you ask them, they say: "People differ in their temperaments, and it is our duty to provide for their temperaments." But the believer has authority over himself and holds its reins, so there is no need for you to accuse anyone so long as the matter is in your hand, and you must carry out the authority which Allah has given you. If you do so, then in your hand is ninety-five percent of the movement of life, and the remaining five percent belongs to others.

Then, what is permitted of singing is conditioned by a time that is not a general characteristic nor a pressing habit upon a person that he makes his constant practice; therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Refresh the hearts hour by hour."

As for these singers, men and women, who introduce into singing what is not part of it of movements and dances, they do not realise that they...

You were called to truth and you became arrogant. And if you were arrogant in your essence, you would not have resorted to falsehood to purchase it. So then: how can you be arrogant about accepting the truth while you are in need even of falsehood?

And why are you arrogant when you do not possess the elements of arrogance? It is known that a person becomes arrogant about accepting a thing only if he has its like. So how, when you possess neither its like nor anything less than it?

So then: your arrogance is misplaced. The arrogant person is always one who is heedless of Allah, because he looks at himself in relation to people, and perhaps he has among the qualities something by which he is arrogant over people, but he is heedless of Allah. Had he kept in mind the majesty of his Lord and His greatness, the Exalted, he would have been ashamed to be arrogant. Greatness (al-kibriyāʾ) is the attribute of magnificence and of majesty that befits none but Allah, the Exalted. So His greatness, the Exalted, is an honour for us and a protection that keeps us from being slaves to other than Him, the Exalted.

Therefore we hear in the colloquial proverbs: "Whoever has no great one, a great one is bought for him." So if I have a great one, people fear me and I take refuge in him. Likewise the believer takes refuge in the greatness of his Lord, because the greatness of Allah is over all, and everyone before Him is equal; no one can raise his head before the Truth, the Exalted.

So then: His greatness, the Exalted, is for our benefit.

And this arrogant one, who is arrogant about hearing the verses, ﴿as though there were deafness in his ears﴾ [Luqman], that is: heaviness and deafness. ﴿So give him tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Luqman]. We know that glad tidings (bushrā) are only of good, for they are the announcement of a pleasing matter whose time has not yet come, just as you give your son the good news of success before the result appears.

As for giving tidings of punishment, it is by way of mockery and derision toward them, as you mock the negligent pupil by saying to him: "I give you the good news that you failed this year." Using "glad tidings" for punishment is like suddenly moving him from expansion to constriction, and in this there is pain to the soul before he suffers the pain of the punishment. The pupil to whom you say "I give you good news" rejoices in the good news and thinks he has passed, but he is surprised by the reality that pains him.

The poet depicts for us this shock of feeling in his saying:

*As a cloud flashed for thirsty people one day, then when they saw it, it dispersed and cleared away.* (1)

*So I became, from Layla at dawn, like one who grips water, which the fingers' gaps betrayed.*

Therefore they say: there is nothing more harmful to the soul than an enticing beginning followed by a despairing end. We have previously illustrated this with the prisoner whose thirst reached its limit, and he hoped for the jailer, until the jailer brought him a cup of water. He rejoiced and was glad, and thought his jailer was a good and noble man. But when he raised the cup to his mouth, the jailer struck it from his hand and spilled it on the ground.

There is no doubt that this is more painful and more severe upon the prisoner's soul. Had the jailer refused from the outset to bring him water, it would have been less painful. This act they call "despair after raising hopes": he began with him a hope-raising beginning and ended with him a despairing conclusion. We seek refuge in Allah from being seized after being extended.

The benefit of faith lies in acting in accordance with its demands; otherwise, what is the use of your believing in many things if you do not put what you believe into practice, and do not translate it into deed and reality? Therefore, if you are content with faith merely as a word spoken without action, you have made faith a proof against you rather than a proof in your favour.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 31, verse 9:

Then Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿Abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

When we reflect on these verses, we perceive Allah's mercy toward His servants, even toward the disbelievers among them who went astray and led others astray. Yet Allah is merciful to them even in the way He describes their punishment. Do you not see that Allah, exalted is He, described their punishment as humiliating and painful, but did not mention eternity (khulud) with it, as He mentioned eternity here for the bliss of the Gardens? Likewise, the punishment came in the singular form, whereas the Garden came in the plural form. Then He informed about it that it is ﴿the promise of Allah, true﴾ (Luqman).

The word "wa'd" (promise) is always used for a good that will come to you. We have said that the servant makes promises and may not fulfil them, because he does not possess all the means of fulfilment. As for the promise if it comes from Allah, it is certain, because He, glorified is He, possesses all the means of fulfilment, and no one can prevent Him from accomplishing what He wills, since He, glorified is He, has no partner. This is like the man who wanted to disparage another and said to him: "The proof that Allah has no partner is that He created you. For if He had a partner, he would have said to Him: there is no need for you to create this one."

Therefore, the Truthful One, glorified and exalted is He, teaches us to attach to our promises the words "in shā' Allāh" (if Allah wills), so that we are fair to ourselves before people, and we are not accused of lying if we do not fulfil them. Then I may say: "I intended, but Allah did not will it," and so I have left the matter in the court of your Lord, mighty and majestic is He.

By this will, Allah has spared people from the tongues of people. If you assign me something and I do not accomplish it for you, know that it has a decree with Allah that has not yet come to its time, and know that the matter is not decided on earth until it is decided in heaven. So do not become angry or unjustly lash out at people, for matters are not by the will of people, but by the will of Allah.

Therefore, when you intercede for your brother in the attainment of some interest and it is accomplished through you, the true believer who believes in the decree of Allah behaves courteously toward Allah and says: "It was accomplished through me, not by me," meaning: Allah willed that it be accomplished, so He honoured me by not having me speak about it at the time of His will, exalted is He. Likewise, the believing physician says: "The cure came through me, not by me."

Had people understood the meaning of the decree of Allah, they would have found rest. When you see the diligent person of glory pushed aside and distanced, and you see the idle and the hypocrite brought near and raised to the highest positions, do not become angry; and if you do not respect him for his own sake, then respect the decree of Allah concerning him.

Matters do not run in Allah's dominion like a mechanical movement, but by the decree of Allah, who raises whom He wills and lowers whom He wills, and He, glorified is He, has the consummate wisdom in this and that. Otherwise we would say, as the philosophers say, that Allah, exalted is He, created the cosmic affairs and then left them to people to run.

The Truthful One, glorified is He, did not leave these affairs, as evidenced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He creates what He wills. He bestows females upon whom He wills and bestows males upon whom He wills. Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ (al-Shura).

So after this verse, no one should say: "So-and-so does not bear children," or "so-and-so does not bear," because these are sublime wills of Allah, exalted is He. And if the barren woman had respected the decree of Allah in her barrenness, Allah would have made every child she sees her own child. Since Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿He bestows﴾ (49) (al-Shura), the matter in all its states is a gift from Allah, exalted is He, and no one has any part in maleness, femaleness, or barrenness. So why do you accept Allah's gift in males but do not accept Allah's gift in barrenness?

We have previously spoken of the burying of daughters before Islam, because the girl would not ride horses, nor defend her people, nor bear arms, etc. When Islam came, it forbade that, honoured women, and elevated their status; yet preference between son and daughter has continued to exist.

Now a fabricated conflict has flared up between the partisans of men and the partisans of women, and Islam is innocent of this conflict, for man and woman in Islam are complementary, not opposed. It is strange that we see among women one who is fanatical against men, while she goes mad if she does not bear a son, and this is their testimony to his superiority.

It is as though the Truthful One, blessed and exalted is He, teaches us that whoever respects His decree in the begetting of daughters, Allah says to him: "You have respected My decree, so I will give you according to My decree," and Allah gives him sons, or facilitates for his daughters husbands who will be more dutiful to him than his own sons and more obedient.

Then do you not see that Allah, exalted is He, placed females first in the giving, saying: ﴿He bestows females upon whom He wills and bestows males upon whom He wills﴾ (al-Shura, 49)? Why? Because He, glorified is He, knows people's love for males: ﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female, his face darkens and he suppresses his grief. He hides himself from the people because of the evil of what he has been given of good news﴾ (al-Nahl, 58-59).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ (Luqman, 9): the Mighty who is not overcome, and who does not consult anyone about what He does. ﴿The Wise﴾ (Luqman, 9): that is, in promising, and in fulfilling the promise.

Then the verses move to one of the proofs of innate faith in the existence of God:

﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see, and cast into the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with you, and He scattered therein creatures of every kind. And We sent down water from the sky, and made grow therein every noble kind of pair.﴾ (31:10)

First: The Truth, glory be to Him, mentioned a cosmic sign that none of the disbelievers or atheists has claimed for himself. It is a sign that exists and is witnessed. After He, glory be to Him, said, "I am the Creator of the heavens and the earth," no one opposed Him, and no one came forward to say, "Rather, I am the Creator of the heavens and the earth."

We have already said that a claim stands in favour of its holder and maker if no one contests it. If this claim is true, and the Truth, glory be to Him, is the Creator, then the matter is settled. If there is another creator besides Him, glory be to Him, then where is he? Did he know that someone else had taken creation from him? Why did he not contest it and defend his right? Or did he not know anything, so that he is a god "sleeping on his ear"? In both cases, he is not fit to be a god who is worshipped.

Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ (3:18). This is the self's testimony to itself, and no one has contested it, so it stands in favour of its holder until someone contests it.

We have already illustrated this, and to God belongs the highest likeness, with a group of people who sat in a gathering. When the gathering broke up, the owner of the house found a wallet whose owner he did not know. He contacted those who had been in his gathering and asked them about it, but none of them said it was his. Then one of them knocked on the door and said: "By God, I forgot my wallet here." There is no doubt, then, that it is his, since no one else among them claimed it.

God, exalted is He, says in establishing this matter: ﴿Say: If there were gods with Him, as they say, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ (17:42). That is: they would have gone searching for the one who took creation and people from them, and took divinity from them.

If they say, "We are gods, but above us is a greater god who refutes the truth they claim," (the verse says): ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves; nor would I take the misleaders as helpers﴾ (18:51).

As for His saying, ﴿without pillars that you can see﴾ (31:10): as you travel around the globe from its north to its south and from its east to its west, you find the sky overhanging you, and despite the vastness of the sky, you find no pillars holding it up. The phrase ﴿that you can see﴾ carries two meanings: either it truly has no pillars, or it has pillars but we do not see them. ﴿Without pillars that you see﴾ means: we see no pillars for it. But the reality is that it has pillars that you do not perceive with your senses or your measures.

If you ask, "What are these pillars we do not see?" Some say they are gravity, but this view is far from correct, and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿...and He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ (22:65).

So we can only say that it is held by the power of God. And so that we do not get confused about how this happens, God brings this matter near to us through an example we can observe: the birds, which God holds up in the air of the sky: ﴿Have they not seen the birds, made subservient in the atmosphere of the sky? None holds them up except God...﴾ (16:79).

In another place the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ (35:41). So He, glory be to Him, holds them by a law, but we do not know it nor comprehend it.

In language, "sky" (samaʾ) is everything that is above you and overshadows you. So the cloud that rises above you and that you see close to you is counted as sky, as God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky﴾ (31:10), and water descends from the cloud, not from the lofty heavens. The difference between them is that you see the cloud in one place and not another, and you see it scattered and split, whereas the upper sky is of one form, and you see no rifts in it.

When the Truth, glory be to Him, spoke of the earth and the sky, He said that there are seven heavens, and did not say seven earths. Rather, ﴿and of the earth the like of them﴾ (65:12) indicates that the earth is seven like the sky. Although the sky is everything that overshadows you, the earth is everything that bears you up. But where are these seven earths?

The Noble Qur'an has informed us that the heavens are seven, and the Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that he passed through them on the journey of the Ascension (miʿraj), and said regarding the first such-and-such, and regarding the second such-and-such. Since the sky is everything that overshadows you and the earth is everything that bears you up, the creatures in the first heaven, for example, have as their sky the second heaven, and as their earth our first heaven, and so on and so forth.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And cast into the earth firm mountains﴾ (31:10). That is, the firm mountains fixed and firmly joined to the earth, so that they do not become loose. The reason for creating the firm mountains upon the earth is ﴿lest it should shake with you﴾ (31:10), that is, lest it incline and convulse with you. Had the earth been created in a state of stability, it would not have needed anything to stabilise it.

Therefore: the earth is in motion, and the mountains were created only to stabilise it and control its movement. This verse thus indicates the truth of the theory that the earth rotates. Likewise in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass as the clouds pass﴾ (27:88).

Therefore the mountains have a motion linked to the motion of the earth. If you ask, "Why do we not see it?" We say: because being in one place prevents you from perceiving this motion, for one who is fixed in one place does not notice differences in the appearances of things relative to himself.

Suppose this mosque that gathers us were designed in the shape of a millstone turning with us. Would we feel its rotation while we rotate with its rotation? We do not feel it. Why? Because our positions relative to one another are fixed and do not change. Likewise our position in relation to the place; therefore we do not feel the motion. But we do feel motion when we measure a moving thing against a fixed one. If we opened the door, for example, or the window, and saw what is outside the mosque, then we would feel that we are moving.

Therefore, no one on the earth can feel its motion, because he moves with it. And since the mountains are pegs in the earth, and the mountains, that is, pass as the clouds pass, the earth must also pass and move with the same motion. The motion of the mountains is not intrinsic; rather it follows the motion of the earth. The Truth, glory be to Him, likened the motion of the mountains to the motion of the clouds, and the motion of clouds is not intrinsic either, but follows the motion of the winds.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, mentions another reason for creating the mountains: ﴿and He scattered therein creatures of every kind﴾ (31:10). We have already explained that the mountains represent stores of sustenance by which human and animal life is sustained, which comes from crops. We have also shown that the outer layer of the mountains is broken down by weathering, then rainwater carries it to the valleys, increasing the fertility of the earth year by year. From the mountains also water forms in rivers or in the channels of the earth, and we bring it out when we need it.

Among His wisdom, exalted is He, is that He made the mountains firm and stable, and made them hard; for if they were fragile, the rains would dissolve them and crumble them within several years, and then the earth would be deprived of the fertility it draws from the mountains. Therefore God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We send it down only in a known measure﴾ (15:21). With the increase of population, the fertile area formed by the silt that breaks off from the mountains increases year after year.

And if you wish, read His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days, and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance...﴾ (41:9–10).

So God made the mountains firm so that the earth would not convulse with us, and made them solid because they are the store of fertility that supplies us with the crops by which our lives are sustained.

By God's mercy toward man, He made in him an innate drive to preserve life: if food or drink is withheld from him, he is nourished from the reserve in his body. He first draws on fat, then on flesh, then on bone. Therefore we say that bone is the last store of sustenance in the human body. In light of this we understand the words of our master Zakariyya: ﴿Indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾ (19:4).

That is: he has reached the last stage of the stages of preserving life.

So it was part of God's mercy to His creatures that even man's greed for food and drink is a mercy to him, since the excess beyond his energy and need turns into a store in his body. When the ways are cut off to him, or food and drink are unavailable, he draws on what is in his body.

Likewise, by God's mercy toward man, He made him able to endure without food for up to a month, and to endure without water from three days to ten, according to the reserves of food and drink in his body. As for air, he cannot endure without it beyond the span of an inhalation and an exhalation. Therefore His mercy and wisdom in His creation are manifest in that He did not make the air the possession of anyone: if your enemy owned it, you would die before he was pleased with you.

His saying, ﴿and He scattered therein creatures of every kind﴾ (31:10): "scattered" (baththa) means spread out. A dābba is everything that crawls upon the earth. Crawling is according to what moves on the earth. Everything that walks on the earth has a sound of movement, which we hear in a large animal, for example, but do not hear in an ant, for example. Yet the ant also has a movement, as evidenced by our saying: "So-and-so hears the footstep of an ant." Thus it has movement upon the earth, but which ear is able to hear it?

His saying, ﴿of every kind﴾ (31:10): "kull" here signifies a comprehensive whole that includes everything that has motion and crawling upon the earth. That is, everything that may be called a dābba, from the ant or viruses now up to the largest animal on the earth. The particle "min" (of) moves from the small to the large, and thus indicates comprehensiveness.

Among these creatures are some that God has made lawful and some that He has forbidden. Therefore some say: since God has forbidden these animals, what is the need for creating them? Is every created thing edible?

No. Not every created animal is edible, for it has another function to perform.

If you reflect on what has been forbidden to you, you will find that it serves you in another respect. Some of it sustains the animals you do eat; some has a property you need for purposes other than eating. The serpent, for example, we see only as a harmful creature, but have we not now needed its venom, making it a beneficial antiserum? Do we not benefit from its skins? And so on. If we do not eat it, we benefit from its existence in other respects.

Likewise the pig, for example. Some say: since God has forbidden it, why did He create it? Glory be to God! Did God create everything for you to eat? It is not necessary that you eat everything, for God has given you your food that suits you. Do you eat petroleum, for example? How can you, when we see that even cars, trains and airplanes each have their suitable fuel? The car that runs on petrol, for example, does not run on diesel, and so on. Your Lord gave you your sustenance just as He gave other creatures theirs.

Therefore, if you look into a forest that human hands have not touched, you will find in it all kinds of animals, birds, beasts, insects, and so on, without finding in it any foul smell or repellent sight. Why?

Because among the animals there is an ecological balance: the weak and the sick are food for the strong, and the excrement of one animal is food for another, and so on. They are governed by instinct, not by reason and choice.

Everything in which man has no hand proceeds according to the most precise order, so you will find no corruption in it at all unless the hand of man has reached it. You may go to one of the gardens or parks on Sham el-Nessim, for example, to see what human hands leave behind in nature.

But why was man described with this description? Why was his existence linked with corruption? We say: because he handles things without the law of their Creator, and if he handled things by the law of the Creator, mighty and majestic, he would not have caused this corruption in nature.

We have already shown that man has no power over anything of God's creation except...

Then Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿This is the creation of Allah. So show Me what those besides Him have created. Rather, the wrongdoers are in manifest error.﴾ (31:11)

The address here is to the stubborn and the obstinate who deny the signs of Allah. ﴿This...﴾ (31:11) refers to what has already been mentioned to them: the creation of the heavens without pillars, the creation of the firm mountains and the animals, the sending down of rain, and the bringing forth of vegetation, and so on.

All of this is ﴿the creation of Allah﴾ (31:11), and no one has claimed it for himself, nor does Allah have any partner in it. ﴿So show Me what those besides Him have created﴾ (31:11), that is, those whom you have taken as partners with Allah: what have they created?

They have no answer to this question, since there is no reality for them to point to as evidence, and not even stubbornness can help them, because the truth is clear (abla¹) and falsehood is confused (lajlaj²). For this reason we have not heard from them any voice, and none of them has dared, for example, to say that our gods created the mountains, or the sun or the moon. So they were unable to respond despite their disbelief and obstinacy.

In His response to them, Allah, glorified is He, shows them that the matter does not stop at their inability to create, but that they do not even know how they themselves were created: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, nor was I one to take misleaders as helpers﴾ (18:51).

In Allah's words ﴿nor was I one to take misleaders as helpers﴾ (18:51) there is evidence of the truthfulness of the Qur'an and a manifestation of its inimitability. Allah, glorified is He, has informed us that there would appear misleaders who would lead people astray on the question of creation and turn them away from the truth with false speech.

Indeed, Allah spoke the truth, and we have heard from these misleaders someone who says that the earth is a piece of the sun that separated from it, and we have heard someone say that man originally is a monkey, and so on. Had it not been for these statements and others like them, this verse would not have been borne out, and the enemies of Islam would have come to us saying: Where are the misleaders about whom the Qur'an informed us?

So every speech that contradicts ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ (31:11) is, as it were, a misleading speech, and these misleaders, in their heedlessness and without intent, end up confirming the words of Allah: ﴿nor was I one to take misleaders as helpers﴾ (18:51).

We find this matter also in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), where from time to time someone emerges who denies the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah and says: Between us and you is the Book of Allah; whatever is lawful in it we make lawful, and whatever is unlawful in it we make unlawful.

To this we say: Glory be to Allah! It is as if Allah had appointed you as proof of the truthfulness of His Messenger, for the Messenger informed us about you and about what you would say concerning his Sunnah, when he said: "Soon a man will be reclining on his couch, narrating a hadith from me, and he will say: Between us and you is the Book of Allah; whatever we find in it of lawful we make lawful, and whatever we find in it of unlawful we make unlawful." (³)

The meaning of ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ (31:11) is: His creatures. ﴿So show Me what those besides Him have created﴾ (31:11). We will not ask you for a creation like the creation of the heavens and the earth and the mountains, nor for sending down rain and bringing the earth to life with vegetation. Rather, create the least of the things that exist which you see, and there is nothing less than a fly: ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ (22:73). Rather, even more than that: ﴿And if the fly should snatch away from them something, they could not retrieve it from it. Weak are the pursuer and the pursued﴾ (22:73).

Then Allah, glorified is He, concludes the verse with His words: ﴿Rather, the wrongdoers are in manifest error﴾ (31:11), that is, an error encompassing them from every direction. Manifest error that encompasses someone leaves no hope of guidance, so these people will not be guided. Your duty, O Muhammad, is only to be patient in your call until Allah gives you in exchange better than these people, and they become soldiers for you who believe in you and support your call. And so it was.
