Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 31, verse 18:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people, and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾ (18)

Meaning: "tusa''ir" comes from "al-sa'r" (ṣa'r), which is originally a disease that afflicts the camel, causing it to incline its neck. The proud person who inclines his cheek and turns away from people out of arrogance is likened to it. We hear in colloquial speech that people say of the arrogant man: "So-and-so walks with his neck twisted."

So the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And do not turn your cheek toward people...﴾ (18) [Luqman]. The choice of this particular comparison is as if Allah, glory be to Him, is alerting us that arrogance and turning the cheek is a disease: this is a physical disease, and this is a disease of character. The poet was alert to this meaning and said:

"So leave every tyrant to time, for time straightens the crooked neck."

That is: if the people of the age are unable to straighten the arrogance of the proud man, leave him to time, for it is worthy of straightening him. We often see examples of people who were haughty and tyrannical, and who now cannot stand or sit upright, nor can one of them even drive a bird away from his face.

A person usually does not become arrogant except when he feels in himself a superiority over others. The evidence: when he sees one above him, he humbles himself and straightens his bearing. We may illustrate this with the "fatwa" (a local strongman, "fityah") of the neighbourhood who sits in the café, for example, with one leg over the other, indifferent to anyone; but when another, stronger "fityah" enters upon him, you find him spontaneously straightening his sitting posture.

This matter explains to us the saying: "Beware the evil of the one to whom you have done good." Why? Because the one you have done good to once passed through a period when he was weak and needy while you were strong, so you did him a kindness, and you rendered him the favour that set his life right, so that you now have a hand over him. Whenever he sees you, he is reminded of the period of his weakness. Moreover, days are alternating turns among creatures; the weak becomes strong and loves to exalt himself among his acquaintances. Yet he must humble himself when he sees the one who did him good; it is as though the presence of the benefactor is the obstacle before his exaltation and pride. Therefore it was said: "Beware the evil of the one to whom you have done good."

Furthermore, the one who is arrogant should be arrogant over something inherent in himself, not over something bestowed upon him. If you see in yourself a distinction over others, then consider what they excel you in; and when you look at creation and the Creator, you find every creature beautiful to Allah.

Thus is related the story of the slave-girl who used to play with her mistress, adorning her and praying for her to have the dream-husband, the proper young man. Her mistress said: "But I pity you, for you are black, and no one will look at you." The slave-girl said: "O my mistress, remember that your beauty does not appear to people's eyes except when they see my ugliness. What you see as ugly is in its essence beautiful, for it displays the beauty of Allah, the Exalted, in the openness of power." Then she said: "O woman, do not anger God with any of this. Do you blame the design, or do you blame the designer? Had you known the trust in me in dealing with you in everything I am charged with, and the lack of trust in you in what your father charges you with, you would have known in what respect I am beautiful."

The poet says in this meaning:

"The face is white like dawn, and the hair is black like night;
two opposites, when they combine to beauty, the opposite shows the beauty of its opposite."

Allah the Exalted teaches us this lesson in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people; perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women; perhaps they may be better than them.﴾ (11) [al-Hujurat].

So if you see a person beneath you in something, search within yourself and look: for he is certainly superior to you in something else, and by that the balance is restored.

Allah the Exalted distributed endowments among all creatures, and He did not favour any one of them over another; and as we have said: the sum of each person's endowments equals the sum of the other's endowments.

We have already mentioned that a man said to Luqman: "We have known you as a black slave, thick-lipped, serving so-and-so and tending sheep." Luqman said: "Yes, but I carry a white heart, and from between my thick lips there comes out sweet, delicate speech."(1)

Luqman is sufficiently honoured in that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned his words, related them in His Qur'an, and made them eternal, recited and worshipped by; and Allah preserves them by preserving His Qur'an.

We have a remark on His saying ﴿And do not turn your cheek toward people...﴾ (18) [Luqman]: the word "lil-nas" (toward people) here has a bearing. It is as though Allah says to the one who turns his cheek: do not lead people into disobedience and rebellion against the decrees of Allah by your arrogance toward them and by displaying your own virtues while concealing theirs. For you may encounter a weak-faith person who rebels against Allah and objects to His decree in you when he sees you arrogant and lofty while he is lowly and humble. So if you are a professional in turning the cheek and a "kayf" (a show-off) in arrogance, let it be between you and yourself, as, for example, standing before a mirror and doing whatever pleases you, of what satisfies this disease in you.

It is as if the words ﴿toward people...﴾ (18) [Luqman] mean that Allah wants to prevent people from seeing you in this condition, because you may tempt the weak in their religion and in their contentment with their Lord.

Then Luqman says: ﴿And do not walk through the earth exultantly...﴾ (18) [Luqman]. Al-marah is strutting and swaggering. Your Lord does not prohibit you from walking on the earth, but He prohibits you from walking the gait of one who looks down on people, self-admiring. Allah commands us: ﴿So walk in its pathways and eat of His provision; and to Him is the resurrection.﴾ (15) [al-Mulk].

So walking on the earth is required, but in a specific manner: walking a straight, moderate gait. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, saw a man walking in a languid, dying manner, and rebuked him, saying: "What is this languor, O man? Allah has granted you health; keep it for your old age."

He saw a man walking the gait of the "shuttar" (i.e., highwaymen), and forbade him from leaping, running, or hastening in his walk.

So the requirement in walking is the form of moderation. Therefore it will come in Luqman's words: ﴿And be moderate in your walking...﴾ (19) [Luqman], meaning: do not walk the gait of the exhausted, languid one, nor leap the leap of the people of evil and highwaymen.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾ (18) [Luqman]. The "mukhtal" is one who finds a distinction for himself in the eyes of people; the "fakhur" is one who finds a distinction in himself. Allah, the Exalted, does not love this nor that, because He, glory be to Him, wants to govern people by the principle of equality, so that people know that He, the Exalted, is the Lord of all, and He, glory be to Him, is alone the Proud in the universe. When greatness belongs to Allah alone, this protects us from anyone else being arrogant over us, in accordance with the saying of the versifier:

"And the prostration you shun among a thousand prostrations, in it is salvation."

So our prostration together to the true God protects us from prostrating to every tyrant and every arrogant oppressor. Thus the pride of the Truth, blessed and exalted, is for the good of the servants.

(1) Cited by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (7/5317): "He said to a man who was looking at him: 'If you see me as thick-lipped, from between them comes delicate speech; and if you see me as black, my heart is white.'"

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says on the tongue of Luqman, peace be upon him:

﴿And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice. Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys. (19)﴾

Al-qasd (moderation): it is the approach to the matter, an approach that has no excess towards either extreme, meaning balance and moderation. This applies to walking. ﴿And lower your voice...(19)﴾ [Luqman], i.e., lower it, and what suffices of delivery is what reaches the ear.

But why did the Qur'anic context combine walking and voice? They said: because a human being has objectives in life, and he reaches these objectives either by walking, for I do not walk to a place unless I have an interest and a purpose in it, or by voice, for if I cannot walk to it, I call to it with my voice.

So: either you go to your objective, or you summon it to you. And moderation (qasd), meaning balance in the matter, is required in everything, because everything has two extremes, and in one of them there must be exaggeration and in the other shortfall. Therefore they said: both extremes of the course of matters are blameworthy.

Then He, glorified is He, says, likening the raised voice to the voice of a donkey: ﴿Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys. (19)﴾ [Luqman]. Some people understand this verse in a way that wrongs donkeys, for humans usually accuse donkeys of stupidity and humiliation. Therefore the poet says:

And none submits to oppression aimed at him
except the two most humiliated: the mare of the tribe and the stake.
This one is tied up for abuse in its entirety,
and that one is pulled, and no one pities it.

We object to the poet for describing the "mare of the tribe", meaning the donkey, as humiliated, and pairing it in this attribute with the stake, which has become a proverbial example of humiliation, so much so that they said "more humiliated than a stake", because you strike it with a heavy tool until it splits in two, so it does not object to you, nor complain, nor does anyone come to its aid. The donkey is subjugated, not humiliated; rather, it is made submissive to you by God, glorified is He.

If we consider the nature of donkeys, we would find how wronged they are at the hands of humans. You make the donkey carry manure and filth, and you leave it to sleep in the mud, and it does not object. You make it a mount for riding, so you groom it and place a saddle on it and a bridle in its mouth, and it hastens with you wherever you wish without complaint or objection.

They also said regarding the wisdom behind the donkey's loud bray: the donkey is short and not tall like the camel, for example, and when it goes out to seek pasture, a hill or a tree may conceal it, so its owner cannot find it unless it brays. Its voice is thus one of the natural instruments of the desert and a necessary feature of its needs, suited to its nature.

Therefore we must understand the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys. (19)﴾ [Luqman]. The braying of the donkey is not disagreeable on the donkey's part; rather, what is disagreeable is that a human's voice resembles the voice of a donkey. So the donkey's bray is a perfection in it, while your voice that resembles it is a blameworthy disgrace in you. Otherwise, what is the donkey's fault?

You notice the camel, for example, which is larger and stronger than the donkey: if you load it with a load, when it finds it heavy it (grunts, yunaʿʿir). As for the donkey, you load it beyond its capacity and it carries on without speaking or showing objection. The donkey, by what God has placed in it of instinct, looks, for example, at a "canal" (qanah); if it is within its capacity it jumps across, and if it is beyond its capacity it refuses, no matter how much you force it to cross.

As for the human, his conceit in himself calls him to bear what he cannot bear. It is said that when the donkey brays, it sees a devil. And we have learned by experience that animals, including donkeys, sense earthquakes before they occur, and that they break their tethers and flee to open ground. This was observed in the Agadir earthquake in Morocco, and we noticed it in the earthquake of the year 1992 CE, when the animals in the zoo became agitated shortly before the earthquake.

Moreover, if the donkey takes you along a road, however long it may be, it brings you back by the same road without your directing it, and goes to it again without passing beyond it. But those who are prejudiced against donkeys say: "Yet it is a donkey, because it does not act on its own; it simply places one step after another." We say: rather, the donkey is praised even if it does not act on its own, because it is governed by instinct.

Likewise is the case in the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not carry it is like the likeness of a donkey carrying volumes... (5)﴾ [Jumu'ah].

So when do we affirm and negate an action at the same time? The meaning: "they carried it" means they knew it and preserved it in their books and in their hearts, and "they did not carry it" means they did not fulfil its due in carrying it and did not act upon it. Their likeness in that is ﴿like the likeness of a donkey carrying volumes... (5)﴾ [Jumu'ah]. Does this count as a reproach to the donkey? No, because the donkey's task is only to carry. What is blamed in them is that they carry the Book of God and do not act by it. The donkey's task is to carry, while your task is to understand what you have borne and to discharge it.

Thus moderation in voice is something the believer should adorn himself with, even in prayer and worship. God, glorified is He, teaches us: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor be silent in it, but seek between that a way. (110)﴾ [al-Isra']. As for what you hear of loud shouting through loudspeakers and wailing all night, it brings us nothing but the anger of the sick, the anger of the employer, and others. We have indeed conducted a count and found that those who come to the mosque have not increased by anything because of the microphones.

Likewise, those who raise their voices in reciting the Qur'an in mosques, thereby disturbing people. Every person should be left to draw near to God by what is light upon his soul: this one wants to pray, this one wants to glorify or seek forgiveness, and this one wants to read in the Book of God. So why do you compel people to your own voluntary worship?

After the verses presented to us a portion of Luqman's wisdom and his admonitions to his son, we move to a new cosmic meaning:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and has completed His favours upon you, outward and inward? Yet among the people is he who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book.﴾ (31:20)

*Taskhir* (subjugation, the placing of things at man's service): it is submission to the Supreme Creator in a task that a thing performs without choice regarding its movement from it, as Allah subjected the sun and the moon, and so on. Despite the fact that many people turn away from Allah and from the way of Allah, the sun has never refused in any day to shine upon them, the air has never withheld itself from them, the earth has never grudged them its bounties, nor the sky its water. Why? Because they are subjected and have no choice.

We should not understand from this that Allah subjected these creatures against their will. That is a superficial understanding of this matter, in which some hold that only man was given choice. The reality is that the entire universe has been given choice. This is clear in the saying of Allah, the Exalted:

﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it; and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant.﴾ (33:72) [Al-Ahzab]

So, all of them have been given choice: the heavens, the earth and the mountains were given choice and they chose to be subjected, having no will of their own, while man was given choice and chose to be free, because he has a mind with which he thinks and compares alternatives.

The meaning of subjugation is that you cannot make subject to yourself, by your mind, your will or your method, those things in the universe that benefit you. The proof of this is that if you catch a bird and confine it in a cage, preventing it from flying in the sky, and you want to know whether it is subjected to you or not, and whether keeping it is lawful or unlawful, then open the door of the cage for it. If it remains in your company, it is subjected to you, content to remain with you because of the morsel it eats or the place you have prepared for it. But if it leaves and abandons your company, know that it is not subjected to you, and you have no right to make it tame against its will.

For this reason, our master ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by a small boy who was playing with a sparrow. He wanted to teach him a lesson while he was still soft clay, so he persuaded him to sell him the sparrow. When ʿUmar bought it and it came into his possession, he released it. The boy said: "By Allah, I never again confined an animal to make it tame."

We have previously spoken about the matter of subjugation, and how Allah subjected the huge camel so that a small child can drive it, whereas He did not subject, for example, the flea to you. If Allah had not made these creatures tractable and placed them in your service, you would not have been able to subjugate them by your own strength.

As for His saying, ﴿and has completed His favours upon you, outward and inward﴾ (31:20) [Luqman]: *asbagha* means to complete and perfect. Among its uses is the saying of Allah about our master Dawud (David): ﴿that make full coats of mail﴾ (34:11) [Saba'], meaning sturdy, well-fitted coats of mail that protect the wearer from sword blows and spear thrusts. Coats of mail are placed over the vital organs of the body, such as the heart and the lungs. Allah taught Dawud to make coats of mail in the shape of the ribs, not smooth, but with projections on which the force of a blow shatters, so that it does not slide and strike another place.

It is narrated that Luqman saw Dawud, peace be upon him, kneading iron in his hands, and he was amazed. But he did not hasten to ask him about what he saw, and he gave him time until he had finished making the coat of mail. Then he took it, put it on, and said: "What an excellent war garment you are!" Luqman said: "Silence is wisdom, and few are those who practise it." Thus this wisdom has continued to be repeated until the end of time.

So the meaning of "completed His favour upon us" is that He has perfected it in a manner that encompasses every movement of your life, and constantly supplies you with the necessities of this life, so that nothing is lacking for you, neither in sustaining life nor in sustaining the species, because the One who created, glorified is He, knows everything that the creature needs.

As for when you see a shortfall in some respect, the shortfall comes from the side of people, in that they have not drawn out what the universe offers, or they have drawn out its bounties but been stingy with them and grudged them to others. This is the affliction of the world in the modern age: you find a people who sat idle and were lazy about research and drawing out, while others strove, but they withheld the fruits of their striving. Sometimes the bounties overflowed for them to the point that they threw them into the sea and destroyed them, at a time when others die of hunger and poverty.

So the affliction of the world is not that it finds nothing, but that it does not use well what it finds of bounties and of the means of sustenance that Allah placed in His universe. The saying of Allah, ﴿and has completed His favours upon you, outward and inward﴾ (31:20) [Luqman], is a truth that no one denies. Do you deny that He created you, and created for you from yourselves spouses, that you may find tranquillity in them? [Cf. 30:21]

Do you deny that He created the heavens with what is in them of stars and galaxies, and created the night in which you rest, and the day in which you strive for your livelihood? Then (consider) what He has created in yourselves of outward and inward senses, and made for each of them a domain and a task it performs without your noticing, what Allah has placed in your body of signs and marvels. Every day knowledge brings us something new of the favours of Allah upon us, in ourselves and in the universe around us.

So the meaning of ﴿outward﴾ (31:20) [Luqman] is what has become apparent to us, and ﴿inward﴾ (31:20) [Luqman] is what we have not yet reached. Among the favours of Allah upon us are those we perceive, and among them are those we do not perceive.

Consider, for example, the two kidneys and how they work within you, filtering the blood of urea, purifying it, while you are unaware of it. When scientists first thought of an alternative to them in case of their failure, they designed an apparatus that filled a large room, half the size of this mosque, with equipment to do the work of the kidneys. Then it became clear to them that the kidney is a collection of a million cells, of which only a hundred work in rotation.

They said: kidney failure is the failure of the hundred cells assigned to the work to be activated at the appropriate time; that is, the first hundred have performed their task and stopped, without the other hundred being activated. Among the engineering of the human body is that Allah created two kidneys for man, so that if one is disabled, the other performs its role.

As for the inward favours, some of them are discovered in the future of the days, as signs and favours. Some years or centuries ago, we did not know anything about electricity, for example, nor about cars and means of transport, the age of the wheel and steam, and so on.

All of these are favours apparent to us now, though they were hidden before. Scientific activity, research and drawing out from the data of the universe made them apparent. When you calculate what knowledge has revealed of the favours of Allah, you find it to be about 3%, while 97% is what man has come to know by chance.

We have said that the secrets and favours of Allah in His universe are without end. No one should say that what Allah placed in the earth of signs and secrets has finished its task, for it remains as long as the life of this world lasts, and it will not cease except when the saying of Allah is fulfilled:

﴿until, when the earth has taken its adornment and become beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it as a harvested field, as if it had not flourished yesterday.﴾ (10:24) [Yunus]

In the Hereafter we shall see other signs of Allah and other wonders of His creation. It is as if the Truth, the Exalted, is saying to us: "You have seen My signs in this world and taken them in. Come, let Me show you the great signs that I have prepared for you in the Hereafter."

In the Hereafter I shall bring you into another mode of existence, in which you eat without excreting, do not feel pain, years pass over you without your growing old, and you do not fall ill, nor die. In this world you lived by My means; but in the Hereafter you will be with Me, with the Causer Himself, glorified is He, and you will have no need of means: neither the sun, nor the moon, nor... and so on.

For this reason we say: it is part of the etiquette of scholars to say "we discovered," not "we invented," because the signs and favours of Allah are buried in His universe and need someone to search for them and infer them from the data and premises that Allah placed in His universe.

We have previously said that every secret of Allah's in His universe has a birth like that of a human being. When its time comes, Allah makes it manifest, either through the research of scholars, or else it comes by chance, as a generosity from Allah, the Exalted, to His creatures whose efforts fell short of reaching His secrets in His universe.

In this there is an indication and a preface to our believing in the unseen that Allah has told us about. Since we have seen His favours that were hidden in His universe, we ought to believe in what He tells us of the unseen, and take from the observable a proof of what is hidden.

Consider the saying of Allah on this matter: ﴿and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾ (2:255) [Al-Baqarah]. That is, He, glorified is He, willed that this unseen should exist and should become manifest to people after it had been hidden. If it coincides with research, it comes with the research; if it does not coincide, it comes by chance and without causes. The proof is that He attributed the encompassing of knowledge to them.

As for the unseen that has no premises by which one can reach it, and which no one knows except Allah, it is what is meant by His saying: ﴿the Knower of the unseen, and He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has approved﴾ (72:26–27) [Al-Jinn].

And He, glorified is He, said ﴿outward and inward﴾ (31:20) [Luqman], because the outward draws our attention to belief in Allah, the Necessarily Existent, the Highest, while the inward He stores up for whoever comes after; then He stores up another storing, so that it will not appear except when we are with Allah in the Garden of Allah.

Scholars have tried to enumerate the favours and signs, outward and inward. The outward are what He gives us apparently in this world, and the inward are what Allah has told us of. For example, when you want to strive in the cause of Allah, you prepare its equipment of weapons and soldiers and so on, and you take the means; then Allah supports you with hosts from Him that you do not see, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels: "I am with you"﴾ (8:12) [Al-Anfal].

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed us of some of these inward favours. He said: "The believer has three things that are his and are not his." That is, they are not from his own deeds. The first: the believers pray for him (for forgiveness). The second: Allah has made for him a third of his wealth that he may bequeath, that is, he does not leave it to the heirs, but he disposes of it himself. The logic would be that you benefit from your property while you are alive; when you pass away, nothing of it remains for you, and it passes to the heirs, whom Allah distributes it among by the inheritance He has ordained. So it is a favour that you are permitted to dispose of a third of your property by bequest, to expiate your misdeeds and purify your sins. The third: Allah, the Exalted, has concealed your faults from His creatures, and if He had exposed you through them, your family, loved ones and relatives would have cast you off."

Among the greatest favours upon us is that Allah has veiled the unseen from the creatures of Allah. If you were given the choice: "Would you like to know people's unseen and for them to know yours?" there is no doubt that he would never agree to that. The Prophet (ﷺ) clarified this matter in his saying: "If you were to uncover one another, you would not bury one another." That is, if what is hidden of a person's unseen were revealed, and people knew what is in his heart, they would leave him if he died, not burying him, and they would say: "Leave him to the dogs to eat him," as a recompense for what he did.

But because Allah veiled people's unseen, we find that even a person's enemy hastens to carry him and bury him, as the poet said: "Death has erased the causes of enmity between us." Yet it is folly on man's part to search out the faults of others and pursue their shameful secrets. Would you be content for people to treat you in kind, pursuing your shameful secrets and seeking out your faults?

Furthermore, one bad deed that people know about you is enough to make them lose interest in all your good deeds. Allah, the Exalted, wants people to benefit from one another, so that the movement of life may be enriched.

Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And among the people is he who disputes about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an illuminating Book﴾ (31:20) [Luqman].

Luqman, peace be upon him, began to be amazed and wanted to ask him, but his wisdom prevented him from asking. When he finished it, he poured it over himself and said: "What an excellent war garment this is!" Luqman said: "Silence is part of wisdom, and few practise it. I wanted to ask you, but you were silent until you spared me the need."

Then the Exalted says:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ (31:21)

The phrase ﴿what Allah has sent down﴾ is general and includes all the revealed Books. The closest meaning to it is that we say: follow what Allah sent down upon your messengers in whom you have believed. If you did this, you would accept the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah and acknowledge his mission.

Or the meaning may be: ﴿Follow what Allah has sent down﴾, that is, to correct your situations; present it to your minds and reflect upon it.

But their reply comes: "Rather" (bal), and bal indicates their turning away from what Allah has sent down: ﴿we follow what we found our fathers upon﴾. In another verse: ﴿They say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ (2:170).

So what is the difference between wajadna (we found) and alfayna (we found/encountered), which have one meaning? They said: because the lifespans of the addressees differ in their companionship with their fathers and their being influenced by them. Some of them lived with their fathers, imitating them for a short period, and some of them lived alongside the fathers for a long period until they became attached to what they were upon and loved it. Therefore the Qur'an said once "alfayna" and once "wajadna."

The second difference we notice is in the concluding phrases of the two verses. Once it says: ﴿Even though their fathers did not understand anything nor were they guided?﴾ (2:170), and once it says: ﴿Even though their fathers did not know anything nor were they guided?﴾ (5:104).

So what is the difference between "ya'qilun" (they reason) and "ya'lamun" (they know)?

The one who reasons is the one who can, by his intellect, derive things. If he does not have the deductive intellect, he knows the matter from one who derives it. Accordingly, knowledge ('ilm) has a wider circle than reason ('aql), because reason knows what it itself has reasoned, whereas knowledge knows what it has reasoned itself and what others have reasoned. So His saying "ya'lamun" also includes "ya'qilun."

Therefore: when reason is negated, knowledge is not negated, because someone else deduces for you. The simple rural man, for example, can operate a television, benefit from it, and move among its channels, while he knows nothing about how the device in front of him works; he learned from the one who teaches him. A person knows what he reasons by himself, and knows what others reason and convey to him. Therefore the negation of knowledge is a sign of total ignorance, with which there is no hope of setting the situation right.

We also notice that the Qur'an says here: ﴿They say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ (31:21), and in another place it says: ﴿They say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon"﴾ (5:104). Their saying "we follow what we found our fathers upon" indicates the possibility of their following the truth; the denial here is simple. As for those who said ﴿Sufficient for us﴾ (5:104), meaning: it is enough for us and we do not want anything else, this indicates intense denial. Therefore in the first verse He negated reason from them, and in the other He negated knowledge from them, so the ending of each verse comes appropriate to its beginning.

Here the Exalted says in the concluding phrase of this verse: ﴿Even though Satan was inviting them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾ (31:21), because their fathers did not go to what they went to—worshipping idols and disbelieving in Allah—except through the whispering of Satan. So Satan is a common factor between them and their fathers.

This shows us that the gates of misguidance come sometimes from the self (nafs), and sometimes from Satan, and by both the light of faith and the light of the method is obscured in the heart of the believer.

We have previously explained that you can distinguish between a sin that comes to you from Satan and one that comes from your own self. Satan wants you to be disobedient in any way whatsoever; if you resist him in one direction, he moves you to another direction. As for the self (nafs), it desires one specific sin in which it stops and does not turn away from it. The self inclines toward one particular thing, and it is difficult for it to repent from it, and every soul has a point of weakness or a desire it prefers. Therefore some people have, as we have said, "tuffashat" (a sort of detector) for souls, because through practice and experience they know the point of weakness in a person and reach him through it: this one's entry point is such, and that one's entry point is such.

But we see many who fall into sin attribute the responsibility to Satan, so one of them says: "Satan misled me," and does not blame himself. This is contradicted by the Prophetic hadith about Ramadan:

"When Ramadan comes, the gates of Paradise are opened, the gates of Hell are closed, and the devils are chained." (1)

If all sins came from Satan, we would not see any sin in Ramadan, and no crime would be committed in it. But since sins occur in it and crimes are committed, there must be another cause besides Satan, because the devils are shackled and restrained in it.

1 Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih (1079), and by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad (2/357), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

Then the Truthful One, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good has grasped the most reliable handhold. And to Allah is the outcome of all matters.﴾ (31:22)

Meaning: whoever wishes to free himself from disputation without knowledge, without guidance, and without an illuminating Book, let him submit his face to Allah. For Allah, exalted is He, said in another verse: ﴿He said: "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them."﴾ (38:82-83) Then He made an exception of them: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ (15:40).

And He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Indeed, My servants – you have no authority over them.﴾ (17:65)

The meaning of ﴿submits his face to Allah﴾ (31:22) is that he sincerely devotes his worship to Allah alone. By this he is in the company of Allah, and whoever is in the company of his Lord, Satan does not dare to lead him astray, nor does he waste his time with him; rather, Satan turns away from him to a heedless person who can gain access to him. So what saves you from Satan is that you submit your face to Allah.

We have given an example of this: a young child who walks in the company of his father, so none of the boys dares to attack him; but if he walks alone, he is exposed to that and is never safe from it in any way. Likewise the servant, if he slips out of the hand of Allah and His company.

This meaning also occurs in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah...﴾ (2:112). Here He said ﴿إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾ (ilā Allāh, "to Allah"). What is the difference between the two prepositions: ilā (إلى) and the lām (اللام)?

The use of ﴿إلى﴾ (ilā, "to") indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is the goal, and a goal must have a path of guidance that leads to it. As for ﴿اللام﴾ (al-lām, "to/for"), it means direct connection to Allah without cutting a path, and this direct arrival is attained only with a high degree of sincerity to Allah.

So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah...﴾ (31:22) means: you are on the path that leads to Allah, exalted is He, and you are performing what He has obligated upon you.

From the submission of the face to Allah is the saying of the Queen of Sheba: ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ (27:44) The speech here is the queen's speech, so she did not say "I submitted to Solomon," but "with Solomon to Allah," so there is no objection then.

The submission of the face to Allah, or the sincerity of deed to Allah, exalted is He, is a subtle process that requires from the servant a great deal of struggle (mujāhadah), because the soul is never free of lapse, and often a person begins an act sincerely for Allah, but soon the soul intervenes with its love of fame and reputation, so some showing-off (riyā') mixes with the deed, even if slight.

Therefore, our master the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bears this matter on our behalf and reassures the Muslim about his deed, so he says in his supplication: "O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness for every deed I intended for Your sake, but in which something other than You mixed with me."(1)

The Prophet (ﷺ) is not the object of such suspicion, but the Truthful One, glory be to Him, taught him to bear on behalf of his community, just as Allah bore on his behalf in His saying: ﴿We certainly know that what they say grieves you; but it is not you they deny, but rather the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah.﴾ (6:33) That is: you are too exalted in their estimation to be a liar.

And His saying: ﴿فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَى﴾ (31:22) — the word istamsaka (استمسك) indicates strength in the act and clinging to a thing, as we say "tabat fīhi" (he persevered in it); it means seeking to hold fast. Therefore it did not say "masaka" but "istamsaka."

The first sign of holding fast is that you do not feel secure in the weakness of your soul, so your grip on the most reliable handhold is firmer, just as if you were to descend from a high place by a rope, for example, and you grip it tightly, because if you were careless in holding it you would fall. This is evidence of your awareness of your soul's weakness, and that nothing saves you from destruction except that you hold fast to this rope.

Likewise the one who submits his face to Allah and holds fast to the most reliable handhold: he has no means of salvation or protection but this.

The word ﴿بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَى﴾ (31:22): al-'urwah (العروة) is the handle by which one grips a jug, pitcher, or cup, and it is what distinguishes a cup from a glass, for a glass has no handle unless hot drink is to be drunk from it, so they make a handle for it.

The meaning of ﴿الْوُثْقَى﴾ (al-wuthqā, 31:22) is "the firm," and it is the feminine of awthaq (أوثق), as we say: "this is awthaq, and this is wuthqā," like aṣghar and ṣughrā. It means a thing firmly bound to its origin: if it is a bucket, then it is wuthqā with respect to the bucket; if it is a cup, then it is wuthqā with respect to the cup. It is the firmly fastened one that does not break and does not separate from its origin.

The handle varies with what it is fastened to: if a deceitful craftsman makes the handle, it comes weak and brittle, and as soon as you grip it, it comes off in your hand. This is what we call "commercial deception," a trick so that the goods are cheap and the buyer is drawn to them, and then the compensation appears in the rising price of spare parts, as we see in cars, for example: you see the car is cheap, but when you look at the price of spare parts you find it high.

Thus the desire for non-fastening has an aim for the one who benefits from it; but if the one who fastens it is Allah, exalted is He, then nothing is firmer than His handle.

In another place the Truthful One says about it: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah and do not separate﴾ (3:103). So the most reliable handhold is the rope of Allah, firm, which gathers us so that we do not scatter. Therefore, in terminology we call the slit in a garment into which the buttons enter "'urwah" — why? Because it is what gathers the garment so it does not fall apart.

In another verse He described the most reliable handhold with His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿There is no breaking for it﴾ (2:256).

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And to Allah is the outcome of all matters﴾ (31:22). That is: its return. So we do not suppose that Allah created us in vain, or that He leaves us neglected: ﴿Did you think that We created you without purpose and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ (23:115). Had Allah left us without accountability, the deviant who gave his soul its desires in this world would have had a greater share than the upright. Allah would not deceive His servant who believed in Him and followed His way, or hand him over to the oppressors and deviants.

And if the outcome of matters belongs to Allah, that is, in the Hereafter, He leaves us some of that in this world to do with our own selves, so that the course of life may be set straight and its movement bear fruit. Among this is, for example, the examinations we hold for students at the end of the year, to distinguish the diligent from the idle; otherwise everyone would be equal, no one would study, and no one would excel. Therefore the principle of reward and punishment is necessary for life's movement to be upright. If we apply this principle in our worldly life, why do we deny it in the Hereafter?

Is it fitting for this world, which Allah created with such precision and formed with such wisdom, that He leave it thus neglected, where corruption spreads and the corrupters roam freely, and they are not called to account? If this is the outcome, then woe to every believer and every upright person in this world.

(1) Sufyān ibn 'Uyaynah said: Among the supplications of Muṭarrif ibn 'Abd Allāh was: "O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness for what I repented of before You and then returned to; and I seek Your forgiveness for what I pledged to You upon myself and then did not fulfil for You. And I seek Your forgiveness for what I claimed I intended for Your face, but in which there mixed with my heart what You know." Recorded by Ibn Rajab al-Ḥanbalī in Jāmi' al-'Ulūm wa'l-Ḥikam (p. 27); see also Ḥilyat al-Awliyā' (2/207).

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you. To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ (23)

After Allah, glorified is He, had made clear that to Him is the return of everything and the end of all matters, He wished to console His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, so He said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves…﴾ (23) [Luqman]. That is, after what We have said of disputation with knowledge, with guidance, and with the illuminating Book, and after what We have explained of the necessity of submitting one's face to Allah, whoever disbelieves after that, ﴿let not his disbelief grieve you…﴾ (23) [Luqman].

This statement from Allah Most High to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, indicates that Allah knew that His Messenger loved that his entire community be believers, and that he was saddened and pained by the disbelief of those among them who disbelieved. The Qur'an has repeated this meaning in several places, among them the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this statement, in sorrow﴾ (6) (al-Kahf), and He says: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself, [O Muhammad], that they will not be believers﴾ (3) [al-Shu'ara'].

So Allah Most High wants to say to His Messenger: We sent you only to convey; so when you have conveyed, there is no blame on you after that. You often find in the Qur'an a reproach directed at the Messenger of Allah regarding this matter, and it is a reproach for his benefit, not against him, just as you reproach your son who exhausts himself in studying out of concern for him.

Among that is the saying of Allah Most High, reproaching His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: ﴿He frowned and turned away (1) that the blind man came to him (2) And what would make you know? Perhaps he would be purified (3)﴾ [Abasa].

The reproach here is because the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, left the believing man who came to him seeking knowledge of his religious matters, and went to call the disbelievers and those who denied it. It was as if he chose the difficult and arduous and left the easy and simple. Therefore, the reproach here is a reproach for the benefit of the Messenger, not against him, as some people suppose in their understanding of these verses.

Likewise is the matter in the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you…﴾ (1) [al-Tahrim]. Allah reproaches His Messenger because he restricted himself, forbidding for himself what Allah had made lawful for him.

Then He, glorified is He, says: ﴿To Us is their return…﴾ (23) [Luqman]. That is: if you do not see in them the consequence of their disbelief and what befalls them in this world, they will return to Us and We will hold them accountable in the Hereafter, as He, glorified is He, said in another place: ﴿Whether We show you part of what We promise them…﴾ (77) [Ghafir]. That is: you see with your own eyes what punishment befalls them ﴿or We cause you to die, and to Us they will be returned﴾ (77) [Ghafir].

So ﴿To Us is their return…﴾ (23) [Luqman] is the ultimate end. And this does not prevent Us from showing you in them things that manifest Your might and Your victory over them, and their defeat and humiliation before you. This is what happened on the day of the Conquest, the day the Prophet entered Mecca victorious and humble, lowering his head in courtesy and humility, because he knew that victory is from Allah. It was as if the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was saying to the people of Mecca: You wanted sovereignty so that you would be arrogant with it, and I want it so that I may be humble with it. This is the difference between the honour of the believer and the honour of the disbeliever.

Therefore, when the Messenger of Allah gained power over their necks after what they had done to him, he gathered them and said his famous saying: "O assembly of Quraysh, what do you think I will do to you?" They said: "Good, a noble brother and the son of a noble brother." He said: "Go, for you are the freed ones (al-Tulaqa')."¹

You may notice the shift in style from the singular in ﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you…﴾ (23) [Luqman] to the plural in ﴿To Us is their return…﴾ (23) [Luqman], and He did not say "To Me is his return," because the word "man" (من) in the language stands in place of all relative pronouns. If you intend its wording, use the singular; if you intend its meaning, use the plural.

As for the saying of Allah Most High: ﴿so We will inform them of what they did…﴾ (23) [Luqman], it is because We record it against them and enumerate it, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Allah has enumerated it while they have forgotten it…﴾ (6) [al-Mujadila]. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ (23) [Luqman]. That is: the contents of the breasts and what they conceal, Allah knows them, even before they are translated into an observable behavioural or verbal inclination. Allah knows what stirs in their breasts of spite, malice, envy, or conspiracy.

And ﴿ʿAlīm﴾ (119) [Ali 'Imran] is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha) from knowledge, and there is a difference between ʿālim and ʿalīm: ʿālim is one to whom knowledge is attached as an attribute, whereas ʿalīm is one whose knowledge is intrinsic to his essence. Therefore He, Most High, says: ﴿And over every possessor of knowledge is one who knows (ʿalīm)﴾ (76) [Yusuf].

¹ Ibn Hisham mentioned in al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (4/412) that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said after Allah granted him Mecca: "O assembly of Quraysh, what do you think I will do with you?" They said: "Good, a noble brother and the son of a noble brother." He said: "Go, for you are the freed ones."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 31, verse 24:

Then the Truthful One (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says:

﴿We shall let them enjoy themselves for a little, then We shall drive them to a harsh punishment.﴾

Al-Haqq, glory be to Him, makes clear to every believer that he should not be deceived by the state of the disbelievers when he sees them in a condition of comfortable living, abundance, well-being and power, because all of that is a little enjoyment. And al-Haqq, glory be to Him, wants the followers of the prophets to enter the religion on the basis that it is a sacrifice, not a gain.

We have already explained that you can distinguish between the principle of truth and the principle of falsehood by one thing: the beginning of each of the two. The one who enters the principle of truth is ready to sacrifice, while the one who enters the principle of falsehood expects to take his reward. For this reason the early Muslims sacrificed their souls and wealth in the cause of their religion, and left their lands and their children. Why? Because they were charged with carrying out a universal human mission, which only one who is ready to give can bear. As for the advocates of false calls, such as communism and others, they must take first.

Therefore it is narrated that a Companion, when he heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the good news of Paradise, and that between him and it there was nothing but that he fight and be killed, threw away dates that were in his hand, and did not wait until he chewed them, and hastened to the battle seeking martyrdom and desiring what is with Allah. And it was heard from them on the battlefield that one of them would call out: "Blow, O breeze of Paradise!" and another would say: "Indeed I find the scent of Paradise beyond Uhud."

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We shall let them enjoy themselves for a little, then We shall drive them to a harsh punishment﴾ [Luqman], this enjoyment of the adornment of the worldly life is nothing but a gradual leading-on (istidraj) for them, not an honouring. We have said: you do not throw your enemy down from the mat, for example; rather you raise him up and elevate him so that his seizure is painful and severe. Likewise, al-Haqq, glory be to Him, lets them enjoy, but for a limited period, so that their regret will be greater when He seizes them from this bliss.

Read in this meaning the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything, until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair﴾ [al-An'am, 44], i.e., despairing.

The word al-fath (opening) does not yield benefit unless it comes definite (al-fath). We have said: there is a difference between "fataha laka" and "fataha 'alayka." "Fataha laka" means for your benefit; but "fataha 'alayka" means He gave you the world so that it becomes a burden upon your head.

So, if you see this opening for them, do not be deceived by it, and know that they have forgotten what they were reminded of. It has been reported in a narration that when Allah, the Exalted, is angry with a person, He provides him with sustenance from what is unlawful, and when His anger intensifies against him, He blesses him in it.

That is so that he remains in ease, comfortable living and high standing, until when Allah seizes him, the seizing pains him and becomes severe upon him. The seizing of the disbeliever while he is at the peak of his strength and tyranny indicates the strength of the seizing and His power; as for the weak, there is no merit in seizing him, like one who wants to break a record, for example: he aims at the highest figures and breaks them to prove his worth.

From this too we see that when the Qur'an wished to challenge by its eloquence and rhetoric, it challenged the Arabs, who are the people of eloquence, rhetoric and the art of expressive delivery; and there would be no sense in challenging someone who is incapable of speech.

The meaning of ﴿nadtarruhum...﴾ [Luqman, 24] is "nulji'uhum" (We compel them), i.e., We narrow the noose upon them, so that they find nothing but the harsh punishment; or: the period of reckoning and what precedes the punishment is harder than the punishment itself, as came in the hadith that "the sun will draw near to the heads, until people wish to depart, even to the Fire."

The description of the punishment here as {ghalidh} [Luqman, 24] — ghalaẓ (thickness) means thickness, so the meaning is that it is a great punishment, the soul struggling to be shaken free of it with difficulty; for if it were thin, escape from it might perhaps be possible.

Then the context returns to them:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not know.﴾ (31:25)

This is a silencing of them, for they themselves testified that Allah, may He be exalted, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and then He marvels at them because they turn away from worshipping the Creator, glory be to Him, to worshipping one who creates nothing, sees nothing, and hears nothing.

Therefore, after their testimony, and after they said "Allah," the Truthful, glory be to Him, follows it with the words ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah..."﴾ [Luqman], meaning: "Praise be to Allah," because they have acknowledged this against themselves. In our dealings we do the same: when your opponent admits to you, you say, "Praise be to Allah."

This word (al-hamdu lillah, "praise be to Allah") is said in response to many things. When your opponent admits to what you want, you say, "Praise be to Allah." When Allah rescues you from the harm of one of the wicked, you say, "Praise be to Allah," meaning: "Who saved us from the corruption of this corrupter."

So if news reaches us of the death of one of the wretched or of a highway robber, we say, "Praise be to Allah," meaning: "Who rid us of his evil and gave relief to the lands and their people from him." Among this is the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ (6:45) [al-An'am].

It is also said when the wronged is vindicated, when his injustice is returned to him, or when his innocence is shown, as we will say, God willing, in the Hereafter: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has removed from us grief. Indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative.﴾ (35:34) [Fatir].

﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups until, when they reach it and its gates are opened, its keepers will say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it to abide eternally." And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the land, to reside in Paradise wherever we will. And excellent is the reward of the workers."﴾ (39:73–74) [az-Zumar].

So "al-hamdu lillah" is also said when you reach an end that brings you out of the constriction, the anxiety, and the sorrow you were in, and it is said when we enter Paradise and enjoy its bounties, knowing the truthfulness of Allah, may He be exalted, in what He told us of its bounties.

All of this is praise for His blessings, but there is a higher praise. Have you not read the sacred hadith: "Indeed, Allah will manifest Himself to His believing servants in Paradise and say: 'O My servants, shall I increase you?' They will say: 'And how can You increase us when You have given us what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human?' He will say: 'I will cause My pleasure to descend upon you, so I will never be displeased with you after this, ever.'" (1) So what is beyond this pleasure?

He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, exalting [Allah] with praise of their Lord. And it will be judged between them in truth, and it will be said, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ (39:75) [az-Zumar].

This is the highest praise: you were in praise with the blessing, and now you are in praise with the Bestower, glory be to Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ (31:25) [Luqman], meaning those who are heedless of Allah. Or ﴿do not know﴾ means: the true, beneficial knowledge; even if they know knowledge from a book that gives no light, or they know the knowledge that fulfills their desires.

(1) A hadith agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh). It was narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6549), and likewise by Muslim in his Sahih (2829), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and its wording is: "Indeed Allah says to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' They say: 'At Your service, our Lord, and at Your pleasure.' He says: 'Are you pleased?' They say: 'And why would we not be pleased, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?' He says: 'I will give you something better than that.' They say: 'O Lord, and what is better than that?' He says: 'I will cause My pleasure to descend upon you, so I will never be displeased with you after it, ever.'"

For Allah is whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy. (31:26)

Then the context moves on to cosmic signs, and He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy. (26)﴾

After Allah had recorded their acknowledgement and testimony that He, glory be to Him, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, He wished to show us that the heavens and the earth are a container for what is in them. Within them are many things, some of which we know and some of which we do not know. The contained is always more precious than the container. Thus, what is in a (wallet) of money is generally more valuable than the wallet itself, and what is in a safe of jewels, money or important papers is more precious and more important than the safe.

Therefore we have said: beware of making the Book of Allah a holder for something important to you, for it is more precious than anything, so it is to be preserved, not to be used as a place in which to preserve things.

The verse also points to the fact that, just as they acknowledged that Allah created the heavens and the earth, they should likewise acknowledge that everything in them belongs to Him, glory be to Him. This is a rational matter that every person of sound mind arrives at. As long as the heavens and the earth belong to Allah, what is in them belongs to Him. Suppose you own a plot of land and then find something precious in it: in that case it is yours both legally and rationally.

The sensible person should reflect on this matter: to Allah belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth, and among these things is the human being, whom Allah honoured and made the master of all created beings and above them, as evidenced by the fact that they are subjugated to serve him: animals, plants and inanimate matter. Is it right that the servant should be greater than his master, or longer-lived than him?

The sensible person should reflect on this matter and survey the kinds of existence and ask himself: Will the inanimate thing that serves me live longer than I do?

So then: there must be for me another life that will be longer than the life of the sun, the moon and all the other inanimate things that serve me. This can only be in the Hereafter, when the sun will be overthrown, all these creatures will vanish, and the human being will remain.

So then: you are in need of what is in the earth and what is in the heavens of the creatures of Allah, and by Him alone, glory be to Him, do they subsist, although He, glory be to Him, is free of need of them and gains nothing from them. Allah, glory be to Him, created what He is free of need of. Therefore He says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy. (26)﴾ [Luqman], because He, glory be to Him, created with the attributes of perfection, so creation added to Him no attribute of perfection that He did not already have. He is the Giver of life before there existed anyone to give Him life, the Exalter before there existed anyone to exalt Him.

We have said: you do not call someone a poet because you saw him recite a poem, but because he is a poet before he recites it, and had he not been a poet he would not have composed it.

The meaning of ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need..(26)﴾ [Luqman] is: the Absolutely Free of need, because to Him, glory be to Him, belongs all this dominion in the heavens and on the earth. Indeed, a hadith qudsi has come that the heavens and the earth, in relation to the dominion of Allah, are like a ring thrown by a traveller into a desert wasteland. So do not suppose that the dominion of Allah is merely these creations that we know, despite what knowledge has reached in geometry and the calculation of light-year distances.

Allah, glory be to Him, is the Free of need, the absolute Free of need, because He created this creation while being free of need of it, and then gave it to His servants and placed it at their service. It was therefore necessary for this Creator to be praised: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy. (26)﴾ [Luqman]. Ḥamīd is fa'īl in the sense of maḥmūd (praised), and He is also ḥāmid (the One who praises), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Appreciative, Knowing. (158)﴾ [al-Baqarah]. But appreciative of whom?

They said: when a servant thanks his Lord, Allah has taught him that whoever greets you with a greeting, you should return it with something better. Your Lord treats you in this same way: if you thank Him, He increases you, and this increase is a thanks to you for your thanking your Lord, that is, a reward for you.

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿And if all the trees on earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to replenish it, the words of Allah would not be exhausted. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ (31:27)

His words, ﴿min shajarah (from a tree)﴾: here "min" (from) conveys comprehensiveness, meaning from the very beginning of what is called a tree. There is a difference between saying "ma 'indi mal" (I have no wealth) and "ma 'indi min mal" (I have no wealth at all). The first does not preclude that you have negated the category of wealth, both little and much, and you say "ma fi al-dar ahad" (there is no one in the house), though perhaps there is a child in it, or a woman, for example. But if you say "ma fi al-dar min ahad" (there is not a single one in the house), this means that it is empty of everything that is called a person.

The shajarah (tree) is the plant that has a trunk, whose branches have become intertwined, and from this is His saying: ﴿in what they dispute among themselves (fima shajara baynahum)﴾ (4:65).

As for the plant that has no trunk, it is grass or herbage that spreads over the surface of the earth, especially after rain falls. Pens are not taken from this; they are taken from the tree with branches and boughs.

The noble Qur'an has mentioned these two kinds in inimitable speech, when He, glorified is He, says: ﴿The sun and the moon [follow] a precise reckoning. And the stars and the trees prostrate.﴾ (55:5–6). So the sun and the moon are ﴿bi-husban (by precise reckoning)﴾, meaning a precise, firm calculation, because by them the reckoning of time is made. ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾, meaning in submission to Allah, exalted is He.

The word "najm" (star) here may be linked to the sun and the moon, and it may be linked to the tree. It is a word used with one meaning, and it conveys another meaning by its attached pronoun.

The poet has noticed this matter, and he said:

"I watch the star on my journey to you, and my steed grazes on the desert's najm (herbage)."

So he looks at the star of the sky to be guided by it on his journey, and his steed grazes on the star of the earth (herbage). Similarly, there is the word "ayn," which comes to mean gold and silver, and means a spy, and means a spring of water, and means the eye that sees.

The meaning of ﴿and the sea, with seven more seas to replenish it﴾ (31:27): that is, they would assist it and support it if its water ran out. You may ask here: why was replenishment assigned to water and not to trees? They said: because a single pen writes with an immense amount of ink that has no limit, so ink is liable to run out, just as trees grow and renew themselves, whereas the water of the sea is fixed and does not increase.

Read also on this matter: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement.﴾ (18:109).

The number seven here (﴿sab'atu abhur (seven seas)﴾) is not intended as an exact count, but as abundance, as in His saying: ﴿seven heavens﴾ (65:12). These are in our solar galaxy; what then of the heavens in the other galaxies? We know that "sama'" (heaven) is everything that is above you and shades you.

Thus, the number seven is used to indicate abundance. The Arabs regarded this number as the limit of counting, because "'adad" (number) means the numerals that specify the thing counted (ma'dud), so there is a difference between the number and the counted thing. Once we have clarified this difference, we were able to respond to the orientalists on the matter of polygamy. Number means 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, whereas the counted thing (ma'dud) is what distinguishes these numbers.

When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to restrict the absolute plurality of wives, after Allah revealed to him that he should command people that whoever had more than four wives should keep four of them and part from the rest.¹

At that time the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had nine wives, and this ruling did not include them. They said: why did Allah exempt Muhammad from this ruling? How could he have nine while his community has four? They did not notice the matter of number and counted thing: did Allah exempt His Messenger in the number, or in the counted thing?

We say: He exempted him in the counted thing, because He, exalted is He, addressed His Prophet in another verse: ﴿It is not lawful for you [to marry] women after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you.﴾ (33:52). So it was obligatory upon the Messenger of Allah to limit himself to these, not to add to them, and not to marry after them even if they all died.

Therefore, He did not exempt him in the number; otherwise it would have been his right, if one of his wives died, to marry another, and if they all died, to bring others in their place.

You may say: why did Allah make the exemption in the counted thing and not in the number? They said: because the wives of other than the Prophet (ﷺ), if their husband divorces them, may marry someone else; but the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) are "mothers of the believers" and are forbidden to the believers, so if the Messenger of Allah divorced one of his wives, she would remain without marriage.

Therefore the Messenger of Allah was commanded to keep his nine wives, on condition that he not exceed them, whereas it is permitted for others to marry more than nine, on condition that no more than four remain with him. Accordingly, this ruling was restrictive upon the Messenger of Allah in this matter, while it was broad for his community.

We know that most of the Prophet's wives were advanced in age, and some of them had no desire for men, yet they were eager for the honour of being connected to the Messenger of Allah, and the honour of being mothers of the believers. Therefore each of them would relinquish her turn of spending the night with her co-wife, being content with this honour.²

Thus, distinguishing between number and counted thing rid us of the lie of the orientalists, of their prejudice against the Messenger of Allah, and of their accusation against him of polygamy, and that he (ﷺ) broadened things for himself and constricted them for his community.

This matter of number and counted thing is a broad subject that has perplexed even students of grammar. There is no difficulty with the numbers one and two, because we say of the masculine singular: wahid, and of the feminine: wahidah; for the masculine dual: ithnan, and for the feminine: ithnatan. So the number agrees with the counted thing in gender. But the disagreement begins with the number three, where the number is masculine with a feminine counted thing, and feminine with a masculine counted thing. Where does this difference come from?

They said: note that the masculine is the original: therefore the feminine needed a marker, whereas the masculine, being the original, does not need a marker. You say qalam (pen), and you say dawah (inkwell). So the feminine needed a marker, for it is the derivative and the masculine is the original.

Now consider the numbers from three to ten: you say thalathah, arba'ah, khamsah, sittah, etc. The number itself ends in the tā', but it is not the feminine marker, because these are bare numbers without a counted thing. When we want to make this number feminine, and it has a tā', we do not add another tā'; rather we drop the tā', so that the dropping becomes the feminine marker, and the number with a masculine counted thing keeps the tā' according to the original.

What, then, of the number seven in particular? They said: the number one is the origin of numbers, because counting arises from adding one to another. So one is the material from which numbers are formed: you add one to one and say "ithnan," and you add one to the two, and the number becomes three, and so on.

It is known that the least plural is three, and numbers are either even (shaf') or odd (watr). The even is that which is divisible by two; the odd is that which is not divisible by two. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾ (89:3). He began with the even, whose first is two, then three, which is the first of the odd. As for one, we have left it aside, because, as we said, it is the material from which all numbers are composed.

Since Allah, the Exalted, said ﴿By the even and the odd﴾, two is the first of the even, three is the first of the odd, four is the second of the even, five is the second of the odd, six is the third of the even, and seven is the third of the odd.

We have said that the least of the plural is three, so the Arabs regarded seven as the farthest limit of plurality in both odd and paired terms, and they stopped at this number. When they wanted to count beyond it, they used a waw which they called "the waw of eight." The noble Qur'an followed the Arabs in these rules of number.

If you wish, read these verses: ﴿Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened...﴾ (39:71).

As for Paradise, He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups, until, when they reach it, and its gates are opened...﴾ (39:73).

What is the difference between the two verses? Why does the waw come in the second, and why is it not mentioned in the first?

They said: because ﴿futihat (were opened)﴾ (39:71) in the first is the answer to a condition, and this answer was something they used to deny and reject. The condition is establishing: ﴿until, when they reach it﴾ (39:71): what happened? ﴿its gates were opened﴾ (39:71). But did the believers, the pious who go to Paradise, deny this day?

So, ﴿futihat (were opened)﴾ (39:71) here is not the answer, because they know with certainty that it will be opened. The answer comes in: ﴿And its keepers will say to them: Peace be upon you; you are good, so enter it, abiding forever. And they will say: Praise be to Allah who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the earth, that we may dwell in Paradise wherever we wish. How excellent is the reward of the workers!﴾ (39:73–74).

Since the gates of Hell were seven, the waw was not mentioned; but for Paradise the waw was mentioned, because its gates are eight.

Likewise, read the saying of Allah, and notice when the waw is used: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you, submissive, faithful, obedient, penitent, worshipping, traveling, previously married and virgins.﴾ (66:5).

You find the waw before the eighth, because the Arabs consider seven the end of number, with its even and odd components.

As for His saying: ﴿and the sea, with seven more seas to replenish it﴾ (31:27), that is, He makes it an ink for the words of Allah. ﴿The words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ (31:27): the words of Allah are the cause of the existence of wondrous decreed things, because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ (36:82). So every decreed thing from a thing has as its cause "kun" (Be).

Here is a wonder we should reflect upon: Allah says to a thing, which has not yet been created, "Be," as if all things exist in eternity and are written, awaiting this command "Be," and so they come forth into existence, as the people of knowledge say: matters He initiates and does not need to begin.

Thus, ﴿the words of Allah (27)﴾ are "Be" and all of Allah's willed things in His creation, what we know of them and what we will know, and what we will not know until the Hour comes.

Did He not say, concerning the wondrous matter of Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿and His word which He conveyed to Mary, and a spirit from Him﴾ (4:171)? The meaning is that he was not created by the natural means of human creation, from a father and a mother, but was created by this word, "Be." Why?

Because Allah, the Exalted, wishes to establish for Himself the absolute freedom of power in creation, and that He, glorified is He, creates as He wills: sometimes He creates without a father and without a mother, as He created Adam, peace be upon him; sometimes with a mother without a father, as He created Jesus, peace be upon him; and sometimes with a father and a mother, or with a father without a mother, as He created Eve. Thus the rational division exists in all its aspects.

Therefore, with absolute power, causes have no weight: if you wished to become, for example, a drop of water, you would have to bring oxygen and hydrogen in a specific manner for water to come forth, otherwise not. But the Creator, mighty and majestic, creates with things and without things, because things, in relation to Allah, the Exalted, are not agents in themselves; rather they are agents by the will of Allah in them.

Then He, glorified is He, says: {Indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise (31:27)}.
